utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Registrar, can you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Good morning to everybody. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I want to greet everybody on behalf of the Trial Chamber and on my own behalf. As you know, today we are going to have a hearing with the testimony of expert witness Mr. Donia over two days. Mr. Scott, you weren't here yesterday. You want to take the floor? You have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I assure the Chamber that when I'm not in the courtroom I am following things in -- quite closely and am pretty familiar with the examination and cross-examination of Mr. Vulliamy, and I thank the Court's continuing attention to all of these matters. Before the witness comes in, Your Honours, I just wanted to mention a couple of things just to make sure that we are proceeding at least more or less on the same page. In terms of Dr. Donia's report, which has been marked as Exhibit P 09536 in its entirety including the maps and attachments, and I would also mention before continuing, and also Dr. Donia's CV is marked as Exhibit P 09547. Having said that, Your Honours, I just wanted to make sure that my understanding is that all of Dr. Donia's report in its entirety will be in evidence whether I choose to ask questions or give emphasis to certain parts of it or not, and by not focusing or asking questions by any part of the report, that does not mean that any such report -- excuse me, any part of the report is somehow withdrawn or unimportant. But it's my understanding that since everyone in the courtroom including Your Honours and the Defence have the entire report, it is not necessary to cover every word in the courtroom and, therefore, I will be looking at some sections of the report in more detail and other sections may not address at all. I'll leave the report to speak for itself. And of course the Defence can ask any questions on any part of the report as, of course, can Your Honours whether I raise it or not. So I just wanted to be sure that that was the common understanding. If it is not, then obviously I will have to cover the report in much more detail. So, Your Honour, do I have the correct understanding of the nature and use of the report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me explain this to you regarding the procedure followed by this Chamber and other Trial Chambers. When there is a written expert report, once the expert's testimony is over with the examination-in-chief, cross-examination, Judges' questions and redirect examination, the Prosecution or the Defence may ask for the written report to be tendered into evidence, following which the Judges discuss and -- the question of admissibility and rule that the written report is admitted into evidence, then the report receives a final exhibit number, or that the report is not admitted. It may not be admitted because certain parts of the report have been criticised or may not appear to be reliable enough for it to become an exhibit. Then the only thing that is left is the transcript. The Trial Chamber may refer to the transcript in the judgement. So let us be clear on this, Mr. Scott. If the report is admitted, the Judges in the judgement will refer to paragraphs of the said report. If it is not admitted, there will be no reference to it in the judgement. The Judges, in the judgement, will only refer to certain pages or lines of the transcript. So this is how things work, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do understand, Your Honour. Thank you. I have to say, that's is a new approach to me. I've never in my years of practice both here and elsewhere have never had that approach before. It does leave the examiner in a bit of a quandary because now I don't know if I have to then go back and spend time on parts of the report that I had not intended to spend time on. If the examiner does not know what will be included or not included, it makes it difficult to have -- to work through the report efficiently without simply rehashing every sentence of the report efficiently without simply rehashing every sentence of the report. So I'll proceed on the assumption and on the hope -- I will hope, Your Honour, that at the end of the daily the entire report will come into evidence, and you will have the entire report whether I focus on each word or sentence or not. I'll proceed as best I can. Secondly, Your Honour, before we start, in reference to some of the criticisms or comments that were filed by the Defence in connection with the report, I just want to mention one in particular. The scope and nature of the report or the length of the report, if one wants to call it that, let me just say if there is to be any criticism concerning the scope or nature of the report -- I'm not talking about the content of the report. The content of the report, of course, is entirely Dr. Donia's, but in terms of what he was asked to do, he was asked to provide to prepare a very concise and a very readable document for the assistance of the Chamber on some -- certain concepts, persons, organisations, events related to the indictment in this case. It is not as has been pointed out an anything approaching a 500-word analysis or thesis -- page thesis or analysis. It was to provide this Chamber, Your Honours, a short and concise guide, introduction, if you will, to certain basic concepts and events leading up to the key events in the indictment. And in that regard you will note that the report ends in approximately the fall of 1992, and again that was not by accident. That was by design, because it is in October of 1992 that, in terms of the crime base charged in the indictment, that is when we have Prozor, October, 1992. And what Dr. Donia was instructed was to provide a background of certain key events and concepts leading up to but not extending past approximately the fall of 1992. So I thought I'd make that clear so there was no confusion about that. Thirdly, Your Honour, in terms of the report itself, I was concerned that there might be different -- it might have been formatted differently by various people. I know at one time there was discussion on whether there would be end notes or footnotes. Depending on what will format one uses it might affect the page numbers, so if everyone in the courtroom refers to someone says page 6 of Dr. Donia's report and people have different formats or different versions then obviously the page 6 may be confusing because it may not be the same. So I want to make clear that for purpose of the examination I prepared my questions and I believe Dr. Donia has prepared using the version that was filed with the registry some time ago, I believe toward the end of March, in which the end notes, in which the references or end notes are at the back of the document and it's that version of the document that I'll -- at least that I'll be referring to and Dr. Donia will be referring to in terms of page numbers. Thank you, Your Honours. That was the only comments, introductory comments that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. We have indeed the report. It was conveyed to us. There is an introduction and then paragraphs in this report. The paragraphs mention various points, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the peoples, the Croat or Croatian Banovina, Tudjman's point of view, et cetera. Thereafter there is, as you indeed pointed out, towards the end of the report there are references or end notes, and there are appendices, the maps. So I suppose when the witness is in court you're going to put questions to him, but I could do that for you. I guess you get to start by saying good morning. You have drafted a report. Could you tell me what you mean by Bosnia? And I suppose he's going to tell us what he's written and so on and so forth. So I guess that you're going to follow the written report when the time comes for you to put questions. Your colleague yesterday said that you had two hours, you had scheduled two hours for the examination-in-chief, and I suppose that when the witness mentions various subjects you're going to submit documents to him, and you're going to ask him whether certain such and such documents supports his statement, and he's going to say I'm aware of this statement and then we'll have cross-examination to try and contradict this statement. This is how things go. And at the end of the hearing you're going to ask for the written report to be tendered. The Defence unanimously are going to oppose the admission, and then the Judges will deliberate. That's the way things go. There's no secret to it. If everybody agrees on this, we can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, yes. You're correct. What I will do is -- is beyond the introductory part is go to the report and essentially go through the report essentially from beginning to end, but again I will note that there were some sections of the report I did not intend to speak about hardly at all simply because I thought that everyone could read the report for themselves and can ask questions if they wish. If -- if I need to cover the report in more detail based on what Your Honour has told me, then I may have to stop and alter my plans somewhat. I would have to say that with all respect to my colleague Mr. Mundis, the two hours might have been a bit optimistic and it will indeed be optimistic if I have to cover the report in more detail than I had anticipated, but we'll do our best to present it as quickly and efficiently as possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the French interpreter says if I have to go into more detail about the report. You are not the one talking about the report. The witness will speak about it. You put questions. You are not the expert, the witness is. We agree on this don't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I meant was, direct the witness to give a more detailed treatment in court. That's what I meant to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, yes, this is what I understood. Madam Usher, can you please bring the witness in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Before your solemn declaration, I'd like you to introduce yourself, surname, first name, date of birth, and current occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Robert Donia. I am currently a research associate at the Centre for Russian and East European studies at the University of Michigan. And you wanted my date of birth, sir? I believe I was born May 30, 1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. For the record I'd like to ask you whether you have testified before, before this Tribunal, and if you have, how many times have you been a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have testified before. I have testified, I believe, in seven other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please sit down. A few introductory remarks before I give the floor to Mr. Scott. You are a specialist with regard to this Tribunal because this is going to be only the eighth time that you're going to testify as an expert, so you won't be surprised by the questions put to you by the Prosecution on your right or the Defence on your left. Unlike other cases, there are many Defence counsel, since we have six indictees with an important Defence panel. As you know, after the examination-in-chief by Mr. Scott, you will answer questions put in cross-examination. The Judges before you can, if they need to, feel the need to, put questions to you. You are an expert. Therefore, you can expect the cross-examination to be hard, but you're used to it. Be aware of the fact that if questions may sound harsh, you are not being criticised as such personally. It is the expert and the content of his expert report that are going to be criticised. This is what happens in all courts the world over. The expert is always under scrutiny and sometimes has to undergo questioning by the Defence and the Judges. But you are very experienced in this matter. Therefore, I'm sure you will be up to the task. If at any time you have any difficulty, need a rest, tell us so, but generally we work for an hour and a half and then we have a 20-minute break and then we resume, except that around 12.00 noon, we have a break, a lunch break of an hour and a half so that you can have a rest, have a bite. This goes also for all the people in this courtroom. And then we start again in the afternoon. If all goes well, you should finish your testimony tomorrow at quarter to two. So we've already used 20 minutes this morning. Without further ado, I'll give the floor to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to just very briefly talk about your -- your background and you were expertise I've had your CV or curriculum vitae marked for identification as P 09547, which everyone in the courtroom has and will provide your background education and publications in more detail, which I will not take the time to cover extensively in court. However, in terms of your education, very briefly, at the end of your CV I note that you have -- you received a doctorate or Ph.D. from the University of Michigan in 1976 and in connection with your Ph.D. the dissertation or thesis that you did is the Politics of Fractionalism, the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your work since then or in terms of its relevance to what brings us here today, this case and matters related to it, I note that you have published three books related to Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I understand your most recent book, titled, Sarajevo: A Biography, has just been published in the last few weeks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you just in only two or three sentences or so just describe to the Judges what that book is about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Sarajevo: A Biography, is a synthetic history of the city of Sarajevo from its founding in about 1450 until about the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. When you say synthetic, sir, maybe you can explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It's a comprehensive history in that it covers an extensive period of time and attempts to bring together, synthesise the various periods of the city's history into one coherent narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In addition to the three books you have written either by yourself or with another, I see from your CV that you have published something approximately like 14 articles related to Bosnia or the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I also note that you have in addition to that written approximately 14 reviews of other people's work, again in connection with the former Yugoslavia, the Balkans, south-eastern Europe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, to follow up on the President's question, in terms of your prior testimony at the ICTY, is it correct, sir, that you testified in the Blaskic days in approximately 1997?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Kordic and Cerkez in approximately 1999?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Simic case in 2001?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Brdjanin case in 2002?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Stakic case also in 2002?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Galic case in 2002?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Milosevic case in 2003?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the Krajisnik case which is still in trial now in July 2005?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can turn then to your report itself, which has been placed -- I think a copy has been placed for your reference on the witness stand. And again for the record this has been marked for identification as Exhibit P 09536. What I'm going to do, sir, and as I've explained to the Judges already, is take you through your report essentially from beginning to end, section by section, although some sections we may virtually skip over, and I'll leave to the Defence counsel and Judges to ask you any questions about those sections as they may wish and direct your attention to some particular parts and items of your report. In that regard if I could direct your attention to section 2, which is the section following the introduction. It's a section entitled Bosnia and Herzegovina. Only two parts from that section that I would like to give some attention to. You mention in this part of your report something called the Independent State of Croatia. Can you please amplify or expand on that, explain to the Judges what the Independent State of Croatia was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Independent State of Croatia was created by the German and Italian occupiers immediately after their conquest of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in fact of the -- of former Yugoslavia in 1941. It was -- it included virtually all of Bosnia-Herzegovina's territory, and the vast majority of the Croatian territories under the -- at the time of the Habsburg monarchy and put these under one set of rulers, the Ustasha, who were Croatian nationalists who had been in emigration in Italy for about a decade and a half prior to 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: So it was a territory that encompassed both the historic Croatian lands and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher, please, to place on the ELMO map 5 from your report. All right. Perhaps if we could just see the top -- perhaps if you could orient the top of the map a bit. Yes, map 5. What you've just said Dr. Donia, is it the correct that the part marked in yellow is what was known as the independent spate of Croatia from 1941 to 1945?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you point -- perhaps on the eastern edge or borders of that entity, could you just point where those are and maybe give us some idea of how that later relates to what was the border, became the border between what was later Bosnia on the one hand and Serbia on the other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the eastern boundary of the independent State of Croatia in the very extreme north went, of course, further to the east, but then followed the Drina River down through a large portion of its eastern boundary. That was, in fact, the boundary by and large between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Kingdom of Serbia prior to 1914, and it became the boundary between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, again after 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So as you said earlier, essentially the Independent State of Croatia during this time essentially covered the entire territory of what became post-war as Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then -- and did that entity or that territorial arrangement ended at the -- with the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask the usher's assistance to put on map number 6. Just by way of a quick reminder and overview, is that then a configuration of the former Yugoslavia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it existed after the war after the end of the independent State of Croatia until approximately 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Follow the same boundaries again, at least the northern, say, one-half to two-thirds of the boundary between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbia, again following the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We can move on to section 3 of your report. What I'd like to focus your attention on in the next few minutes, sir, is on page 5 of your report. You talk about essentially the fact that of the three principal et thing groups the Croats, Muslims, and Serbs lived in close proximity to each other and in Bosnia-Herzegovina to varying degrees "making it impossible to delineate on a map a sizeable, contiguous territory inhabited by members of only one group." Could you tell us a built more about at that and what the implications of that were for any nationalist groups that were trying then to carve out some sort of compact, homogenous areas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Through a combination of religious conversions and migration, these three peoples had intermingled in almost all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In many areas there was a mix of Muslims and Croats, many other areas a mix of Muslims and Serbs. In still other areas there were makes tour of all three groups, including most of the major cities, particularly Mostar, Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, other -- other cities. There are small areas that are ethnically monolithic, if you will, in a couple of municipalities in Western Herzegovina or -- Western Herzegovina and in north-western Bosnia which is -- that enclave being Muslim, but by and large through the republic as a whole, the intermingling is such that drawing lines on a map is a futile exercise in terms of trying to create a monolithic or mono-national territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You mention on page 6 of your report on the bottom half of the page, based on the 1991 census, the approximate percentages of each of the three principal groups indicating the Muslims comprised overall across all of Bosnia-Herzegovina approximately 43.7 per cent, the Serbs approximately 31.4 per cent, and the Bosnian Croats approximately 17.3 per cent. My question about that, sir, just so there is no confusion in the courtroom, those are the percentages across the country as a whole and not in any particular municipality or city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Those are the percentages across the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So for example even though the Bosnian Croats across Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole might be approximately 17 per cent, in some particular locale they might be 80 -- 50 per cent or even 80 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance by putting map number 8 on the ELMO. Can you just briefly indicate -- this is a part your report. Can you just briefly indicate why you included that map and what it indicates?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I included the map for two reasons. Number one, it demonstrates the ethnonational complexity of Bosnia-Herzegovina as we've just outlined. The second reason I included it is, it's very difficult to capture that diversity, those dispersions in any map, and this map comes as close as any to being accurate by municipality in terms of the composition of each. So the primary colour in each municipality indicates the majority nationality or, in the case of the somewhat more faded colours, the plurality, that is majority less than 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And the bars in each municipality indicate the presence of other groups and the percentage that they constitute of the population. So to take just one that's fairly visible here, if we look at Mostar, we see that it has a Muslim relative majority of less than 50 per cent but also has these other groups represented within the municipality as represented by the bar graphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. And focusing -- continuing to focus just as an example on Mostar, if the usher could please put map 7 on the overhead or on the ELMO. Can you again briefly describe for the Judges what this map displace or is intended to indicate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is a map that indicates the geographic dispersion of nationalities within a particular municipality and therefore is very specific as to the concentrations in individual villages and towns, and what one sees with the red being Croats is that there are indeed clusters of Croatian villages to the east of Mostar, but there are also Muslim villages to the west and north interspersed with Serbian towns and villages in that area, surrounding the city of Mostar, which is genuinely mixed, all groups represented and really not distinguished by neighbourhoods or a residential segregation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just have the -- if I could switch to the PowerPoint presentation. We can display that. And for the usher, I'll be finished with the ELMO for at least the time being. Just summarising the points in your report on this section of your report then sir, as you indicated due to these various conditions I think you said a moment ago yourself you referred to the part of your report that says, it's these characteristics which render futile any attempt to separate Bosnia-Herzegovina into homogenous ethnic compact territories; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I don't think it's proper to have a reading, as it were, of the report. I believe the gentleman is here to testify and what we have so far is a reading of the report rather in a clever way, but I would rather have a discourse rather than a reading. We can all read the report. The report has come in. He can discuss it. But I think this is improper use of the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott, try to elicit the witness's answer by asking him to go into detail on given subjects. Then he will be the one who is speaking instead of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 5 of your report, sir, you mention the -- what you called as national identity movements. Could you discuss that in more detail with the Judges, please, what that meant and how that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The late 18th and 19th centuries were characterised by movements led by intellectuals and supported by church authorities in which the Serbian and Croatian nations attempted to define and also then to spread their own identity throughout the community of what were at that time really religious communities. And so by, let's say the beginning of the 20th century we can speak of the national movements of the Serbs and Croats being well developed in Croatia, Serbia, the neighbouring republics, and beginning to develop effectively in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The national movement of the Bosnian Muslims, who later became known as the Bosniaks in 1993, took place somewhat later. So these three national movements did not occur simultaneously. They occurred depending on the strength of the middle class and the articulation of these identities over about a century and a half of time. The Bosnian Muslims asserted their identity in the early 1960s and achieved recognition as a nationality equivalent to the Serbs and Croats in 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 5 of your report, in this regard the last paragraph on that page, you talk about the efforts of the various nationalist movements, and you talk about by means of myth-making, linguistic efforts, commemorations, holidays, and through the national, quote, "national sites." Can you again explain to the Judges what you mean by at that statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, these are Vjekoslav Perica's words and I think he captured in a single sentence this complex process of spreading belief in a national history, in the notion of a common or single language, a set of national heroes and saints whose achievements and births are often commemorated in holidays and then the creation of holidays which honoured a particular event in the national history.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what role if any such things as symbols, flags, certain coats of arms, certain insignia, what -- what role did symbols play in this process?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, these symbols were typically designed by intellectuals but usually drawing been something like a medieval coat of arms or even slogan, and these, I'd say, various symbols including a coat of arms, a national anthem, folk music, folk literature, all these both their literary and very physical tangible evidences of national identity were developed as part of this national awakening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mention in particular among the others linguistic efforts. Can you again explain how linguistics play a role in nationalist movements.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, in the case of the South Slavs, both the Croats and the Serbs in the early decades of the 19th century sought to codify national language which would encompass as many people as possible by definition into their national group. The purpose of that in the minds of the intellectuals was to let's say integrate or fuse the population around a single, standard, uniform national language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apart from those efforts or in light of those efforts, can you tell the Court in general as of the early 1990s, not so much necessarily today but back in 1991, 1992, 1993, how similar or different were the language which we now refer to at the Tribunal as B/C/S or Bosnian, Croat, Serb, how different in practice and day-to-day language were those in the early 1990s? Different or similar?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, they were very similar, and -- and very contested. The intellectuals who were promulgating the notion that the Croats spoke a different language from the Serbs and the Bosnian Muslims promoted that separatism by introducing archaic terms into the language. The Bosnian Muslims did the same thing with Turkish and Arabic expressions. But that was a process that was designed to identify or to promote the separateness. In fact, these languages are wholly mutually intelligible. My favourite illustration of that was the Dayton peace talks at which the each group wanted its own language represented. There were three buttons on the translation panel, and whether you turned to Serbian, Croatian, or Bosnian, you heard the same voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving on. On page 6 of your report you mentioned the fact or situation where both over time, both Serb and Croat nationalists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Wait a minute. Allow me to interrupt you to put a question to the witness. Let me come back to the question you put on page 5. You state in your report that of the 19th century each religious community became the foundation for a sort of lay national identity. You quote an historian, Perica, by saying that the main religious institutions worked together with modern nationalistic individuals on the task of creating nations and nationalities. So what your colleague Perica says as an historian seems very relevant to me and seems to complement what you said. Did you mean in this paragraph to indicate that religions were sort of at the origin of this nationalistic feeling? Is that what you wanted to bring out in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are. Religion and religious tradition were the foundation for these national movements. The national intellectuals who asserted them often denied that there was this highly significant religious identity at the core, but in fact the national movements never deviated terribly far from their religious origins. So, yes, I think the point is well taken that religion is the very foundation from which these movements arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I was asking you also say in your report on page 6 that both Serb and Croat nationalists at various times have claimed Muslims as part of them, if you will. If they were Muslims or either -- in fact Muslims or Serbs, or Muslims or Croats. Did you explain that further to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Let's say in the first -- in the 19th century, the intellectual leaders of these movements were in the business of trying to define their groups as broadly as possible. So, for example, many Serbian nationalists in the 19th century viewed the Croats, or let's say Catholics, as Serbs of the Catholic faith, and likewise Croats viewed Bosnian Muslims as Croats of the Muslim faith. So this, let's say, rivalry over the entire corpus of south Slavs who spoke that language which was called Serbo-Croatian in the socialist period led to -- or ended up in a rivalry about the identity of the Bosnian Muslims. And until the 1960s, most Bosnian Muslims defined their group as a religious community, much as had been the case with Catholics or Orthodox a century earlier. A few of them accepted these overtures from Serbian and Croatian nationalists and declared their nationality as Serbian or Croatian, but the vast majority, particularly those other than elites, rejected these overtures, and, as can be shown in the censuses from the socialist period, would pick just about any identity other than Serb or Croat to identify themselves as distinct from the Serbian and Croatian nationalities. In a sense, this rivalry has really never ended, but by the 1990s, most Croats and Serbs accepted the fact that the Bosnian Muslims were a separate nation and therefore distinct from their particular nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe just for -- just for reference to the point you just made about the census and the -- how the Muslims would categorise themselves you make a statement in your report on page 6 at the end of paragraph -- at the end of paragraph one, I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The socialist Yugoslav state offered a very limited repertoire of possible identities for a census respondent to select, so it changed in each census until 1981, but it was in these categories that the Muslim -- Bosnian Muslim population found refuge in a sense from being forced to declare themselves as Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps you've touched on this a bit already, but if you can say a bit more. What was the -- based on your historical work, what was the purpose or the end that attempted to be achieved by one group or the other as claiming the Muslims to be part of their group?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was the key to demographic control of and majority status in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If the Serbs could succeed in recruiting the Bosnian Muslims for the Serbian nationality, Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a majority Serbian republic. If the Croats succeeded, it would be a majority Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Unless the -- unless the Chamber has other questions on this section, I'm moving on to the next section on the Croatian Banovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just one question for clarification. You said that somehow the Muslims were this challenge or the stake between Serbs and Croats so that they can reach a majority. Is this the way we should understand your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the -- was a primary motivation for the Serb and Croat nationalists to recruit, to pursue the identity of the Bosnian Muslims. Yes, if you would understand my statement to identify the motivation for Serbian and Croatian nationalists to seek to recruit the Bosnian Muslims, that would be what my testimony is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I want to get as full clarity as possible. To put it very bluntly, what you are telling us is this: There is one people, ethnic, pretty much uniform in the territory of former Yugoslavia; however, adhering to different religions, and the leaders of the different religions assisted and complemented by intellectuals built up via the secondary symbols which they created more or less artificially, more or less at the origin artificial nationalism to create a nationalist identity of different groups which originally were one and the same if one abstracts from religion. Is that, very, very roughly simplified, what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may clarify a bit from that. The symbols were not artificial in the sense that they had no foundation in history. Each group looked back to a medieval state, the Bosnian Muslims to a Bosnian medieval state, the Croatian to a Croatian medieval state, the Serbs to a medieval kingdom. So these were not completely artificial, invented coats of arms and symbols. They were, however, selected in some cases redesigned and tailored for the purpose of promoting these national identities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could one mutatis mutandis compared the different kingdoms and states they look back upon to the different Italian states in the Middle Ages, or the German states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Third question. These questions are put to you in order really to get to the core of the matter, to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. President, since being from Hungary and due to the complexities of the history of our region there, I also do have, as far as my mother is concerned, she was born in Croatia, and one of my grandfathers served in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the First World War and fought in the world war between the Italians and Russians, and then my point is anyway that you mentioned previously that during the Yugoslav socialist period of time not too many choices were given to answer in the census who is who, I mean, to which nationality they belong. I do recall that that was a possibility also to choose the, I would say, the "Yugoslav" as being a Yugoslav and not a Serbian or not Croatian or not -- I don't know if Bosnian was -- if that was a possibility to choose Bosnian as a nationality. So my question is: If in the census during that period of time, let's say from the early 1960s to the 1990s, as far as the -- that period of time was concerned, the Muslim Bosniaks, how did they in general put themselves in any categories which you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the 1953 census, as you'll see in my assertion on page 6, the Muslims did in fact opt for Yugoslav undetermined which is a very, to me, meaningless category. In subsequent censuses, the Yugoslav option was used by many people who genuinely believed in the Yugoslav, let's say, state and concept. It was also used by those people from mixed marriages or who simply rejected the national identity, Serb, Croat, or Bosnian Muslim, for one reason or another. The Yugoslav option was selected by -- I think the largest percentage was in 1981 and, I believe, reached about 7 or 8 per cent of the Bosnian population and then decreased somewhat in the 1991 census, because the 1991 census was taken in -- I think at the end of March, 1991, when some of the conflicts were already intensifying in the former Yugoslavia. There was I don't believe in any census ever an option to select Bosnian, but the Bosnian Muslim or Muslim in the ethnic sense or in the national or ethnic sense was an option that was chosen by many Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps just to put a further detail on that, what would be the reason for describing it or why would some people want to state it as Muslim in ethnic sense as opposed to Muslim in what other sense?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, this progression on page 6 here reflects the evolution of what was viewed at the time as the proper way to couch or express this Bosnian Muslim identity. 1961 was prior to the formal recognition of Bosnian Muslims as a nationality. So Muslim in the ethnic sense was viewed in a sense as one step below official national status. In 1971, this has been changed, and Muslim in the national sense is the available category in the census. And then when Yugoslav officials believe that issue is resolved, they simply allow the Bosnian Muslim designation in the 1981 and 1991 censuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there any sense in that terminology, if you know, when people use the phrase Muslim in the ethnic sense, did that also allow for the possibility of someone to identify themselves -- we might say someone considered themselves a Muslim in an ethnic or cultural sense but perhaps was -- did not actively practice the Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can move on, then, to the section on the Croatian Banovina unless the Judges have additional questions on that section?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, the concept of banovina is explained in this part your report called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this section of your report, you talk about the concept of banovina or ban not only in the context of what has been discussed in this trial as the banovina of 1939. So before we get specifically to that, can you just say just generally what the term banovina means or its derivation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is derived from a territory ruled during the Middle Ages by a governor or ban, b-a-n. It was invoked or used in 19 -- after 1929 and the declaration of a royal dictatorship by King Aleksandar of Yugoslavia to create new administrative units which had, in principle, no historical precedent or foundation and which were intended to disregard the national or ethnic divisions within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just focusing on the end of the first paragraph in that section. Do I correctly understand what you mean by that last statement to be that these earlier banovinas, so to speak, well, the ones established around 1929, that these were not in fact based on any particular ethnic groupings or primarily on other considerations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the case. There are historians of various national persuasions who see in this an effort to assure a Serbian plurality in effectively all of the banovinas except the Slovene, the northern, north-western one, but at least in the -- if you look at the map and understand the -- the expressed intent of the rulers, it was to eliminate ethnicity or nationality as a criterion for these administrative boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving specifically, then, to the banovina of 1939. Can you tell us and amplify on your report how that came about, the historical forces or circumstances, if you will, that led to the creation of the banovina of 1939 and what was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There was -- in -- in royal Yugoslavia there was fairly constant discontent by Croatian political leaders with the administrative arrangements that had been created, really from the very -- almost the very first day. These turned into an acute crisis in the late 1930s with the growing influence of Germany and Italy and the possible -- possibility of military action against Yugoslavia by those powers. So the royal leaders authorised Prime Minister Cvetkovic to seek an agreement with Croatian leaders about the constitutional future of royal Yugoslavia, and a series of negotiations took place between Prime Minister Cvetkovic and Zlatko Macek who was the head of the Croatian peasant party and resulted in an agreement which created a Croatian Banovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before moving on, just so the record is clear and so we're all further informed, Mr. -- The Prime Minister Cvetkovic -- Cvetkovic, excuse me, what government did he or nationality, what have you, did he represent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He was a Serb and represented the royal government but clearly was operating and negotiating on behalf of the Serbian component of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you say a bit more about this man named Macek, what his background was? He was the Croat, principal Croat leader in this particular situation in?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. And real little was -- had over the years become an uncontested leader, let's say, of the Croatian political establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how was it then that this particular -- the actual agreement itself was then formed and put into place, if you will? Was there some declaration or how was it this banovina was actually but into place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, this agreement was reached in closed negotiations, and then ceremoniously announced in August of 1939, and then immediately implemented with the changing of boundaries of the banovinas and the implementation of administrative changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For purposes it may come up either today or in the future when there's a reference to the Cvetkovic or Macek he can agreement that is the agreement sir that created the banovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it's much easier to think of it as the "banovina plan" or simply "the agreement."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell the Judges, please, what role if any Muslims played in that agreement or if they had any voice concerning it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The undisputed leader of the Muslim organisation, Mehmed Spaho, was strongly opposed to this agreement and was quite vocal in his opposition to it. He died just a few weeks before the agreement was reached. So there was effectively very little participation by the Bosnian Muslims in the negotiations for the agreement and shortly after it was reached there was quite a bit of opposition to it from various quarters in the Yugoslav Muslim organisation which was the dominant political party of the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I have the usher's assistance, please, to put map 4 from Dr. Donia's report on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if that is happening if I may just raise an observation, Your Honour. I can't help but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can't help noticing at times Dr. Donia is reading his report or parts of it. He has it right there. I would like the testimony to come from his memory if possible. If he needs to refresh his memory that's fine, but I think you know it's either the Prosecutor reading it or the witness reading it, and I don't think this is proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree. I couldn't disagree more. What the whole -- what is the point of an expert referring -- preparing a report that is filed with the Court so that everyone can review it ahead of time? The expert does not come into the courtroom to start all over again from scratch. He has written a report. He has invested in a report, made an effort to collect information, and he was simply to -- are we supposed to put that all entirely to one side and act like it doesn't exist? Of course it's his report and he should be able to refer to it if he wishes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Donia, when the Prosecutor puts a question to you, you answer if whilst looking at us and you just answer by memory, and then if your memory fails, you can refresh your memory by looking at the report. But the main thing is to answer orally, to answer an oral question as it were. Well, of course if you can forget a minor detail, you can of course sort of dive into your report, but normally everything should happen sort of verbally in order to avoid a situation in which you have the Prosecutor reading and the witness reading as well. Of course, this would be saving time, but we have to stick to form. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking now at the over -- or the ELMO presentation, can you tell us, then, what is confirmed -- what is marked in green on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The green body on this map is the Croatian Banovina as it was defined in 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it may assist the Chamber to know perhaps the source of this map. Who -- from where did you obtain this particular map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It's a collection of maps edited by Ljubo Boban who also wrote the definitive work on the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this is not a map that either you or for instance anyone at the OTP has prepared but prepared -- I believe you -- was it a Croat who prepared this map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was published in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned -- before putting the map on the ELMO, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm just looking ahead, Your Honour, for the purpose -- with the assistance of the usher. I think that will be all for now for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned apart from the Muslim concerns or opposition to the banovina plan, was there any opposition to the -- by Serbs or Croats to the plan and, if so, why?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The various political parties took different positions once the plan was announced, and most of the complaints really didn't develop until several weeks and even months after the agreement had been reached, but in general the -- many Croats came to feel that the plan left a lot of Croats out of the banovina, and many Serb political leaders complained that there were too many Serbs within the territory of the banovina, the Croatian Banovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, continuing on, on page 8 and carrying over to page 9 of your report, you make the statement about -- that the banovina continued to be a factor in various thinking or movements, if you will. Can you explain to the Chamber how that was the case, referring to the statement beginning at bottom of page 8 of your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I don't mean to be disputatious, but again I think this is just the way -- if you can't go through the front door now we're trying to get in through the basement window. He can just pose the question. Just an open-ended question, you know? There's no need for him to read the report or to reference it. He can just ask him, you know, very bluntly, and he can help us out. He is a historian after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know the purpose of having a report prepared if the report can't be referred to. Why didn't we just have Dr. Donia come in without a report and just start talking? I just don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can ask him very simply without references the report without having him looking at the report. I believe if you ask him the question, Dr. Donia is perfectly capable of answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. You want the question to speak to the issue of criteria without mentioning page 8 or 9 of the report as such. You could ask him the question, asking him whether there may be criteria, and then he could answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you make a reference to the fact that Croats idealised the arrangements and used the banovina for some -- for additional future purposes after 1939. Can you explain that to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to some Croats and particularly to the era of nationalist revival in the late 1980s and 1990s -- or early 1990s, and then a -- some Croatian nationalists intellectuals and aspiring politicians in the meantime who looked back on this as a -- perhaps not maximum achievement of the Croatian people in terms of having a state but as a far better, far more desirable state formation than existed under socialist Yugoslavia. That would include most prominently at least in retrospect former Croatian President Tudjman and a number of historians and other political leaders who cited this as something they would like to restore or at least idealise as a kind of a general goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you also mention in your report that there is the banovina in fact the banovina of 1939 was referenced in Croatia's constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. For the constitution, it was promulgated in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. That was my next question. If you could tell the Chamber when that language was put into the constitution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think it was June of 1990, if I'm not mistaken. In any case, it was after the elections in the late spring, early summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, and in terms of this, what you've mentioned in terms of President Tudjman in particular, are you the only one -- the only one, sir, to have made that observation or can you tell the Chamber what other either historians or political figures have been involved in the Balkans during the 1990s also indicated this view or had a similar experience in dealing with Dr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, in his book Balkan Odyssey, Lord David Owen makes the observation that he heard this from President Tudjman as something that he himself ideal -- that is Tudjman, idealised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, for instance, other -- did Mate Boban ever refer to the banovina as something that related to what was happening in what became Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. He cited it as a model or, let's say, precedent for the creation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, again I'm going to move past this section to be consistent with what we've done this morning which I think seems to work, in my view at least, reasonably well. If the Judges have any questions on this section, I'll stop before I move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on then, sir, to the next part of your report which begins at page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You provide some background at the beginning part of your report a little bit a limited background about President Tudjman. Can you say anything more about his -- the activities or views that led him to be imprisoned in the former Yugoslavia on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, he was a very vocal critic of the, let's say, socialist system in general as overly bureaucratic, as too authoritarian, and as -- at least in later years, as denying the Croatian nation its due in a political sense. So he was a genuine dissident, even though he had been a general, had served in the Partisans, and was highly regarded for his service to, let's say, socialism and Yugoslavia. He was imprisoned for these views on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you mention then in 1989 he formed the Croatian Democratic Union. Can you tell us more about that, how that came about, any other particular high-profile individuals if any that were involved with President Tudjman in creating that political party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by high-profile individuals. He was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, much of the later political establishment was involved at some level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me strike my -- forgive my words, but can you tell us some of the other individuals besides Franjo Tudjman who were involved in establishing the party in 1989?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I can't give you a string of names right now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this section you talk about President Tudjman's views toward Bosnia. Can you summarise those for the Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He viewed Bosnia-Herzegovina as a territorial intrusion into Croatia, which made Croatia an unnatural geographic and -- let's say, economically unviable geographic territory, and he furthermore believed that the Bosnian Muslims or the vast majority of the Bosnian Muslims by their traditions and language were Croat in ethnicity. So he expressed this -- this view that much of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually belonged to Croatia and that its people were of the same ethnicity as his own, Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber was there anything about that you're aware of the available historical information or the census that we were referring to earlier which would have been contrary to President Tudjman's view that the Muslims identified themselves as Croats, the fact that they often identified themselves as Croat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The indications that I gave earlier whereby the Bosnian Muslims sought refuge from these other rival identities were, I think, evidence that the number of Bosnian Muslims who viewed themselves as Croats was very small. In fact, in one census, I believe it was 1971, it was either 1961 or 1971, you could answer that you were a Muslim and then you also had the option of identifying a nationality, and the number of people who identified themselves as Muslims and Serbs was, I think, about 74.000 out of something like 3 million Bosnians, and for the Croats was somewhat less than that. As I recall, it was around 26.000. So the number of people who in that census format came forward and said they were Croats of the Muslim faith effectively was very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on with the -- President Tudjman's views towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell the Chamber whether he viewed the continued existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a detriment to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He specifically cited the economic factor as impeding the natural development of the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you point out, sir, in terms of your work, any other -- similar to the question I asked you a few moments ago, did President Tudjman express or state these views to other national leaders or historians confirming these views in other statements that he made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Tudjman was remarkably consistent in expressing these views. He first expressed them in a book that was published in the 1970s, translated into English in 1981 as nationalism in contemporary Europe. It's from that book that I've taken the quote that's in the paper, which page I don't know right now, but in addition, he expressed in almost the same words those views to a gathering of Bosnian Croat leaders in his office in December 1991, and he was quoted to that effect again in somewhat similar language by the US ambassador to Yugoslavia at the time, Warren Zimmermann, in his recollection of these events reflected in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we -- I think we're coming up to the break. Before we go to the break, if I could just finish on this. How, again, was the Zimmermann account, if you will, the Zimmermann account of his dealings and conversations with Franjo Tudjman, how does that fit into what you know of the history and literature and that matter in terms of the indications of Franjo Tudjman's views?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, it's consistent with his -- I think with what is reflected in the literature by a number of authorities, namely that Tudjman seems to have been a true believer, a nationalist, which is what one would expect if someone had effectively gone to prison for his views on two occasions during socialism as opposed to Milosevic and, in fact, others, whose views may have been based more on pragmatism and realism than a national, I would say, ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the clock I would indicate this would be, if the Chamber agrees, an appropriate time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Scott. It is now 10.30. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I've been reminded or asked by the translation people, a common problem here at the Tribunal when the examiner and the witness speak the same language is that we tend to go back and forth quite quickly while the translation may still be continuing, so both of us need to provide a bit more of a pause between my answer -- excuse me, my question and your answer, or sometimes my answer. If we could both do that, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, in terms of your report, and I would say for the Chamber, to provide the Chamber the opportunity to ask additional questions, the next section in your report in order starting on page 12 is the Dissolution of Yugoslavia's Central Institutions. And continuing with my approach to the report and time will tell how that's received, but I have no questions on that section. Unless the Judges have any questions on that section, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we're very clear. We do intend to oppose the introduction of the report so later on, you know, Mr. Scott should be fully aware of our position, so -- and there's a possibility, I suspect, since it hasn't been admitted yet, which is why I'm raising all these objections, that the report may not be coming in. So he's moving at his own peril.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will hope to persuade the Chamber of the wisdom of the Prosecution's position on this. You have the report, it was filed some time ago, and everyone in the courtroom can read the report and we've been told not to read it in the courtroom. So it seems we're either all going to sit here and read the report word by word and cover every page and every sentence so that it's in the transcript or, if we're not going to read the report, then I have to rely on the fact of what's in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In a few minutes on this chapter of the Dissolution of Yugoslavia's Central Institutions, the witness could sum up these two pages in the report. So what can you say in a couple of minutes as to the dissolution of these central institutions? I see that you're looking at the report. I mean, you can use your own memory, because you've been a witness eight times on the subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I frankly haven't memorised the report, but I view the dissolution of Yugoslavia's central institutions as having taken place in stages and sort of one institution at a time. The first step in this process was the relative weakening of the federation starting about the time of the constitutional amendments in 1971 enacted in the new constitution of 1974 and then becoming acute with Tito's death in 1980. The second phase really was the rise of Milosevic and his effort to acquire a majority of supporters on the Yugoslav Federal Presidency with a series of demonstrations which are known as the "happening of the people" or the "Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution" in 1988 and 1989, so that by the end of that period Milosevic and his allies held four of the eight seats on the Federal Presidency and effectively could stymie, obstruct any other group from implementing changes or reforms through that Presidency. The transformation of the Yugoslav national army would be a third part of this process, which meant -- by which I mean the transformation of the army from being a true multinational or multi-ethnic force devoted to the principles of socialist Yugoslavia to an effectively single, mono-ethnic institution promulgating, promoting the interests of the Serbian people as interpreted by its commanders. Additionally, the League of Communists, which was always relied upon by Tito and socialist leaders to reconcile differences within socialist Yugoslavia effectively became moribund in January of 1990 with the collapse of agreement or efforts to reach agreement at the 14th extraordinary party Congress in January of 1990. An after that took place the Yugoslav National Army was essentially the only institution in all republics and charged with holding Yugoslavia together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in that section of your report you talk about the fact -- can you tell the Chamber how the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia worked during this time period in terms of the rotation of the president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: When the arrangements were being made for Tito's inevitable death, the succession arrangement was that the Presidency which had at that time nine members would rotate its position of president of the Presidency by republic and autonomous region. So the schedule was drawn up, I believe, two rotations in advance so that on May 15th of a particular year the representative of, let's say Croatia or Slovenia would become the president of the Presidency. The Presidency normally endorsed this rotation with a kind of symbolic vote, but on May 15th, 1991, when Stipe Mesic, the Croatian -- the representative on the Presidency from the Republic of Croatia was due to assume that position, the four -- Milosevic and his allies either abstained or voted no on Mesic's accession, and that effectively left the Presidency without a -- without a leader. Mesic was eventually confirmed after international intervention in the Brioni accord of July 1991, and he served in that position for several months but was effectively marginalised by both the military leadership and the civilian leadership, Milosevic and his allies, of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you say a word or two more about the way in which he was marginalised or how that -- some of the ways that was manifested?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, he was not informed at all about what was going on in the military. He was the commander of a unit or of an army that was fighting against his own people and his own republic. So obviously his orders were completely disregarded, and he effectively stopped trying to function in that capacity and resigned in December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm moving on to the next section unless one of the Judges has any additional questions on this part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next part of your report, sir, talks about the political party formation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990. Can you give us a brief introduction to what -- what the situation had been prior to this time in terms of political parties -- political party or parties in the former Yugoslavia and how that then changed in approximately 19 -- around 1990, particularly in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: From the early days of socialist Yugoslavia in the mid 1940s there was only one political party in power and that was the Communist Party of Yugoslavia which was renamed the League of Communists of Yugoslavia in 1993. It was aided in this socialist scheme of things by a mass organisation which in -- by 1990 was known as the Socialist Alliance. In 1990, with communism collapsing throughout Europe and great popular demand for multi-party elections, each republic of the former Yugoslavia, the legislative body of each republic voted to allow multi-party elections sometime in the course of 1990. That legislation varied from republic to republic, and there was never an agreement on holding an election in all of Yugoslavia for a single Yugoslav leadership. Consequently, this moved forward this process of fragmentation along republic lines. The legislation in Bosnia was -- it under out to be very difficult to reach agreement on that legislation and in fact was passed in two stages. Number one in February of 1990, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina provided for multi-party elections but didn't specify specifically the character of the institutions for which elections would be held, and furthermore, ruled out the policy or legality of parties organised along political -- I'm sorry, national or religious lines. The second set of legislation which was -- consisted of constitutional amendments were passed in -- I think the last day of July, 1990, and that legislation defined the character of the institutions for which the elections would be held. That included a Presidency, a collective Presidency which was very much in vogue at the time, consisting of two Croats, two Serbs, two Bosnian Muslims, and one representative from the category of other. In addition, they provided for the election of a republican Assembly to consist of 240 delegates and representatives to all 109 municipal assemblies and the Assembly of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. You've said that the way that the Presidency was structured at one point in time was that there would be approximately two members of each of the three major ethnic groups and then one other, and this category we discussed earlier today, the "other" category. Was that the original -- always the original concept or are there been earlier a consideration of structuring the Presidency on a proportional -- some proportional basis reflecting population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. As I indicated earlier, there were -- there were many variants that were considered, and the -- one of them, the variants, that was considered was to structure the Presidency proportionally according to the most recent census, which would have been 1981, to have three Bosnian Muslim members, two Serbs, and one Croat. And in the course of negotiations, that was rejected and the agreement was reached pretty much widely shared amongst all the participants in the Assembly that this should be a 2, 2, and 2 and 1 format to provide approximate parity of the three national communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So drawing back on the demographic information that we looked at earlier this morning with Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole representing only approximately 17 per cent of the population, they were nonetheless given exactly equal standing on the Presidency with two persons, the same as the Muslims and the same as the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continue on, please, in just your narrative of how then the parties -- once these structures -- some of these structures were designed how the formation of some of the political parties in Bosnia then took place.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The formation of political parties began well in advance of the legislation that sanctioned them and the determination of the institutions for which they would compete. The organisational activities of all three parties comfortably pre-date the February date for legislation, and in the case of the HDZ, there was considerable -- that is, excuse me, the Croatian Democratic Union, considerable activity in even mid to late 1989 to select key leaders of the party, and there is -- there was also a great deal -- there were consultations and arrangements for the selection of the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party or SDS, as well always the leading Muslim party, the Party of Democratic Action. When the February legislation was enacted, it effectively made illegal some of the activities that these parties were engaged in, or proto-parties were engaged in, and they resorted to meeting in cafes and holding local meetings without registering their parties, and meeting in apartments and so on. And it wasn't until a Constitutional Court ruling of June 1990 that these parties were able to organise legally and hold their founding assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just for reference because it may come up today or in the future. It may have already, in fact. When you talk about the primary Muslim -- so-called Muslim party, the Party of Democratic Action, is that also sometimes known as the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you had the HDZ with it being the primary Croat nationalist party. You would the SDS as mainly the Serb party, and the SDA as being a primarily Muslim party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. There were a host of political parties organised. I think the number was 40 or more. But these three parties emerged as the primary preferred parties of members of the three groups who they claimed as constituents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interject here for one second. Just a point of clarification. I don't recall Mr. Donia saying that the HDZ was the Croat nationalist party. There was an emphasis placed on that, and I want to make sure we're not putting words into the -- he didn't do the same thing with the SDS, and he didn't do it with the SDA, but he's highlighting Croat nationalist party, and I think that's -- there's some -- we have to be very careful not to inject comments into the witness's mouth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will suggest, Mr. President, it is in his report. It's not a secret to anyone that I'm suggesting something that hasn't -- the witness hasn't said in his report that everyone in the courtroom has in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The report is not evidence, Your Honour. I must stress that. It has not been introduced. Had it been introduced, I would not be up here objecting. It has not. The whole purpose is -- is to see if the gentleman can testify. If so, the report may not come in. That's my position.
