Now if there is any other alternative position that the Prosecution has, that's fine. But he's testifying live. He's answering questions. He's doing quite well in fact when he's only -- not referencing to his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I said on several occasions that the objections that are raised are only the result of a question of form, the way in which you put the questions. If you had asked the witness to list the parties who won the elections, he would have mentioned the three parties, and then you could have asked him whether he could define each of the parties. If the witness had said that the HDZ is a nationalist party, it would be his problem, the witness's problem, not yours. So it is the way in which you put your questions that should elicit comprehensive answers by the witness without injecting the answer into his mouth. If the witness says that the HDZ is a nationalist party, then it is him who says so, not you. So I'm going to take up the questions. You heard the objection raised by a Defence counsel. Mr. Donia, regarding the HDZ, what can you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the HDZ was a Croatian nationalist party. The S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop here. You wanted to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me first of all say that when one uses the word "nationalist" in English and it's translated into B/C/S as nacionalisticke, I think it has a much heavier, harsher meaning than it does in English. I use the word nationalistic, but I would almost hope that the translation into B/C/S would be national. Three groups each had a dominant nationalist party. The Serbs had the party of democratic action. The Muslims had the party of -- I'm sorry, the Serbian Democratic Party for the Serbs, the Party of Democratic Action for SDA for the Bosnian Muslims and the Croatian Democratic Community for the Croats. In their approach to their constituencies, in their organisational format, these were very much parallel parties, and they were also parallel in that they achieved virtually complete domination of votes within their respective constituencies and never seriously sought votes from the constituencies of other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall and provide to the Judges, please, information on the -- after the parties were formed -- excuse me just a moment, make sure I'm not -- strike that. We'll get to that eventually. All right. Mr. President, I have no further questions on this section of the report unless the Judges have some additional questions that they would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next section of your report is concerning the Croatian democratic union, HDZ, in Croatia. Can you again summarise for us the formation of that report -- excuse me, that party, how it was -- when it was formed, and who was involved to the extent you recall in -- I mean everyone, of course, but principal players or persons involved in organising that party.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union or HDZ as formed in Croatia in the course of 1989 was very much under the leadership and command of Franjo Tudjman, the former general and dissident. It was his speech at the opening Congress that became the basis for the party programme. He was quite explicit in asserting the sovereignty of the Republic of Croatia and indeed all but moved to assert the independence of the Republic of Croatia in the founding Assembly. That was -- perhaps its most significant platform was, as much sovereignty or sovereignty for the Republic of Croatia and minimum, if any, role for the Yugoslav federation in the future of Croatian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when the founding Assembly of the HDZ was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I don't. I cited in the paper the founding Assembly was sometime I think in late 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections to the gentleman looking at his report to refresh his memory provided he seeks -- you know, he makes a request first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you need to look at your report, Dr. Donia, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, do you need to look into the report in order to find the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do. Look at the first two lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the question was when its founding Congress was held, and I don't believe the founding Congress was held in February. I think it was held somewhat later, perhaps in June or July of 1989. And I don't know if I have cited that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- insist a little bit? In your report you wrote in February 1989, on page 16, second line. Now you say it was later. Can you tell us on what sources you based the date that you give in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several meetings in which party members gathered, expressed an intent to form a party, formed an initiating committee. That was my date for -- that was my first date for February of 1989. The founding Congress was in a sense the last act of party formation. The same was true in Bosnia. There were many months of party formation activities that preceded the founding Assembly. I make that distinction. I think it's an important one. Others really rely heavily on the dates of the founding Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what role Franjo Tudjman played in that party from the time of its formation in 1989 till President Tudjman's death in late 1999?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He was the undisputed leader of the party from the first day til the last and made -- ordered many personnel changes in the HDZ throughout his -- throughout that decade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Mr. President. I have no further questions about this part of his report unless the Chamber would like to ask additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the next section of your report, Dr. Donia, you refer to the Serbian Democratic Party of BiH or SDS. Again, it was my intention not to go into this section, but in light of how things are proceeding, can you give us a summary of what you addressed in that section?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party was organised under the influence of Serbian leaders in the Belgrade leadership, specifically Dobrica Cosic and, to a lesser degree, I believe, Slobodan Milosevic. In the early consultations for the party leadership, they first turned to Nenad Kecmanovic to head the party, who was a former rector, I guess at the time he was rector of the University of Sarajevo, but eventually settled upon Radovan Karadzic as the leader of the party, a psychologist at the university clinic in Sarajevo. He articulated much of the party programme. The party itself was formed in a variety of meetings prior to July 1990, but at its initial or founding convocation in July of 1990, the primary speaker was Jovan Raskovic, another psychiatrist who -- clinical psychiatrist who was well -- very well acquainted with Cosic. The party programme as was to be expected of such a nationalist or national party emphasised the interests of the Serbian people and specifically expressed opposition to a confederal arrangement or other such arrangement which would weaken the central Yugoslav federation. The party's views, in fact, lined precisely with those of President Milosevic of Serbia who had expressed these very similar ideas and emphasis on preserving Yugoslavia and all Serbs in one state at about the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the relationship, if any, between the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serb leadership in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The personal relationship between Karadzic and Milosevic seems to have developed rather slowly, but by the time of the elections, they were in somewhat regular contact, and that relationship grew closer over time. The leadership in Belgrade clearly had an active role in the formation of the SDS in both Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina and continued to, if you will, mentor the party's leaders from the time of -- of its formation through the rest of the -- certainly the -- at least the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to clarify for the record, when you say that the relationship between Karadzic and Milosevic seemed to develop rather slowly, and then you said "by the time of the elections." Can you give us the approximate date of the elections that you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The elections were on November 18, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in reference to the relationship between the SDS party and Bosnia-Herzegovina, you may have said, and if you did and I didn't hear you, forgive me, was there a similar -- was there a party known as the SDS in -- also in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, there was. And the leader of that party, certainly the most charismatic speaker, dynamic personality, was Jovan Raskovic who then became a major speaker at rallies for the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That relationship was largely a personal one and really didn't, let's say, develop until one being dominant over the other, but there was a collegiality between those two SDS parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me move forward, then, to the creation of the Croatian Democratic Union or HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell us how that party -- how and when that party was formed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The HDZ of -- that was formed in Zagreb in 1989 asserted that it was the party of Croats everywhere, and in fact was it -- it's founding Congress was attended by Croats from the United States and Australia and various places in Germany, and Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the course of 1989 and early 1990, the leadership of the HDZ in Zagreb identified and courted a physician from Sarajevo, Dr. Davor Perinovic and invited him to lead the formation of an HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perinovic was in fact the head of the provisional organising committee and was the first president of the party. He was -- he resigned or left his position in -- very early in the game before the elections and was replaced by Stjepan Kljuic who was a popular journalist from Sarajevo and the party then proceeded under his leadership into the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us about what you know about the -- we've talked about the founding assemblies several times now in some of the other party context. The founding Assembly of the HDZ-BiH in Sarajevo, approximately when that was and what happened there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina held its founding Assembly in August of 1990, and the symbology, the heraldry, the symbols and the slogans all represented the parentage of that party in the HDZ as it was organised in Zagreb. Like the founding Assembly of the other two parties, it was held in the Skenderija sports centre. The speakers all emphasised the Croatian nation as a whole, and the Congress really was -- featured pictures of Croatian President Tudjman and the singing of the Croatian national anthem, "Lijepa nasa domovino."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges why it would be a political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not a political party in Croatia but a political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would display the Croatian flag, the photograph of a foreign president, and play the Croatian national anthem?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the party was conceived as a part, an integral part of the HDZ that had been organised in Zagreb. As a nationalist party, it emphasised the Croatian people as a whole wherever they lived, including Bosnia-Herzegovina and thus was effectively an affiliate of the Zagreb party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether in the charter of the -- the political charter document of the HDZ BiH indicated a relationship with the HDZ party in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The founding document specifically identified the party as and integral part of the HDZ as it had been organised in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I have the assistance of the registry in displaying Exhibit P 00013. In other words, 13, Exhibit 13. Sorry, I'm just waiting for it to come up on my screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to page it of that document and move to page 2. For some reason we're not getting the -- I don't know about anyone else in the courtroom but we're not getting -- I'm not getting the feed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I think it would be faster to give a hard copy and to put it on the overhead projector. It would be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll proceed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That took two minutes for it to be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It appears we have it now. Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours, for your patience. On page -- if I can direct the registry to page 2 of that document. Could I ask for the registrar to place this page of Exhibit 13 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So really, it's this system has collapsed; right? It really doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We have it again -- this is the ELMO I suppose, yes. Dr. Donia, if you can assist us by -- if you can find any language on that page, and I have to say working with these various tools I may or may not have given you the correct page, if you can assist us, please, any language which talks about the relationship between the HDZ party and Bosnia-Herzegovina and the party in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In Article 4, the last sentence sums up what I've been pointing out that the Bosnia-Herzegovina HDZ is a constitutive part of the united HDZ organisation whose seat is in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I wonder if the technical booth could assist us by focussing and enlarging the language under Article 4. Well, we'll leave it at that for now, I suppose. Then if I could also ask the witness to be shown Exhibit 31. I don't know if the system is working any better now or not, but otherwise we could have a hard copy of Exhibit 31, in particular, page 2. I'm going to ask the usher to put on -- first to put on the first page of that exhibit, Exhibit 31, which is the Political Platform Of The BH HDZ. If I can have the usher's assistance, please. It's on now. All right. And if we could go to the second page of that document. I don't know if you're able to read it, sir, or not, from where you are, but once again can I ask you to point to any particular language on that page? I'm looking at the top of the page where again it talks about any relationship between the party in Bosnia and the party in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The first sentence reading "The Bosnia-Herzegovina Croatian Democratic Union is an integral part of the single HDZ, just as the Croatian people and its history in Bosnia and Herzegovina are part of the same Croatian national identity." [as read].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: National identity or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: "National entity."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving forward, you've mentioned that the first president of the party, that is the party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was Mr. Perinovic. Can you tell the Chamber what happened with Mr. Perinovic? Did he continue in that position very -- I think you mentioned this briefly but can you just remind us what happened with Mr. Perinovic as the party leader?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He left the party shortly after it was revealed in the press that his grandfather had been a Serbian Orthodox priest and members of his family were buried in a Serbian Orthodox cemetery in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned and then Mr. Kljuic became the party leader?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the -- as the party developed through the time 1991, did there come to be a -- a difference -- different factions in that party in the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Stjepan Kljuic represented a group of Croats who are sometimes identified as urban Croats or Croats who support continued Croatian life within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a rival group, principally associated with Croats living in rural areas, particularly those in living in Western Herzegovina arose under the leadership of Mate Boban in the course of 1991. That faction was -- favoured some sort of territorial unit in which Croatian rights would be realised and was opposed then by those who felt that the best destiny for the Croats lay in their participation in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole since they were so widely dispersed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us how these two factions interacted or how these two factions evolved and what happened over the course of 1991, early 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The territorial faction in November 1991 took the lead in declaring a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and a smaller Croatian Community in the Posavina. In December of 1991, these two factions clashed directly in a large meeting in the office of Croatian President Tudjman, the transcript of which is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And shows that Tudjman's strong preference went to the territorial faction. It really was not until late January, 1992, when this faction announced its intent to take over the party, to take over the leadership of the Croatian delegates in the Bosnian Assembly, those who were HDZ members, and also to assert its supremacy over the Croatian Community of the Bosnian Posavina. In early February this territorial faction effectively ousted Kljuic from the leadership of the party and subsequently became the uncontested dominant faction within the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to the -- the meeting in Zagreb with President Tudjman, can I ask that Exhibit P 00089 be displayed, and in particular the English page number 21. If it's possible to display the English page, it would be page 21 or ERN page 00837881. And, Dr. Donia, in reference, among other things, to the second paragraph beginning on that page saying "It seems to me," is that the language -- some of the language you were referring to earlier a few moments ago when you said that in the course of this meeting President Tudjman came down in the favour of the -- what you've described as the Boban faction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The second sentence there, "It seems to me therefore just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent, internationally recognised Croatia, I believe it is time at that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And he continues in that vein.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I then have the assistance of the registry to go to English page 56 or it would be ERN 00837916. And this also relates back to some of the material we discussed earlier today, but in light of this evolving procedure, if I can ask you to look at the bottom half -- if we could possibly zero in on approximately the bottom half of the page. If we could enlarge that so people can see it. If you can stop there, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. See, he notes in this -- I think it's next to last paragraph, "... the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state, even if possible, is in any case against the interests of the Croatian people and makes impossible the normal territorial establishment of the Croatian states, and creates conditions for the disappearance of what remains of the Croatian," I lose the text here, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher or registry roll up a bit. The other way, please. The other way. Thank you. Can you continue on, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. "... what remains of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina today."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then if I can ask the registry, please, then to -- do roll up higher in the page. In reference to what we've discussed earlier today, I asked you some time ago whether it was Dr. Tudjman, President Tudjman's view that the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a detriment to Croatia. Can I ask you to point particular language on that page again where President Tudjman said this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. As I look at this, it's moving. "Therefore, Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be taken as something God given which must be preserved, and we must especially not forget how harmful it is. "Because of the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia has been put in an impossible situation regarding its territory. Regarding administration, not to mention defence, we cannot establish an independent Croatia such as it is."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In your historical research and work in this area, including in the three books you've published and the other articles you've written, have you come across anything or described anything in terms of the Tudjman government's so-called -- something called a dual-track or two-track policy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact, President Tudjman announced it at this meeting, announced that the approach would continue to run on both a territorial track, which would be the substantive or real policy of the HDZ, and also on what he called a formal or nominal track, which was to support the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the territorial track gradually taking over the more -- the dominant position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina after Mr. Kljuic was effectively removed, can you provide the Chamber with any assistance in terms of what the -- how the Serbs viewed that party -- how the Bosnian Serb leadership viewed that party, HDZ, under Mate Boban's leadership, for example, in relation to either peace talks or to -- in particular the Cutileiro process?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs led by Radovan Karadzic came to feel that they had a companion party in the HDZ and its leaders in that both the SDS and the HDZ came to favour partition schemes for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Karadzic referred to this specifically at a meeting of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in which he noted that the new leadership of the HDZ, that is the leadership as of the purge of Kljuic in early February, 1992, shared with the Bosnian Serbs a notion of how Bosnia-Herzegovina ought to be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the registry to please display Exhibit P 09538. P 09538, and English page 2. I'm asking the usher, Your Honours, to put page 2 of that document on the ELMO. I regret the difficulties that we're having, but we'll do the best we can. If we can have the ELMO viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us what the origin of this document is?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was first trying to get it on the screen if we could. I'm still not getting the broadcast of the ELMO view. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you said a moment ago before I had asked for the exhibit to be displayed, you made reference to a particular meeting where Mr. Karadzic made some comments about this. Which meeting was that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This was a meeting of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a body created by the SDS and Bosnian Serb nationalists in October of 1991, consisting of delegates who were elected, Serbian delegates who were elected to the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1990 elections. The transcripts and minutes of these sessions are now in evidence in various cases before the Tribunal, and in this case we're looking at a transcript of a meeting from February, 1992, in which Radovan Karadzic is expressing his satisfaction with the situation as the negotiating process sponsored by the European Community is going forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can then with that background direct your attention -- if you can follow on that page to about halfway down the page. The paragraph that begins "We don't know much about the Croat delegation," and if that could please be enlarged so that people in the courtroom might be able to perhaps see this a bit clearly, more clearly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see that, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were just there a moment ago with your pen.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Let me move down here and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "We discussed," a little --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. "We discussed a little about the principles on which Serbian-Croatian relations in general could be resolved as regards the Krajina. They think that the best solution would be to relocate population."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hold on one moment, please. Excuse me. Give me one moment, please. I've canibalised my document to give you the page. With the usher's assistance, could I ask you to look at page 1 here. Go to page 1 and we'll come back to page 2. And if I could please ask you to assist us by again enlarging as much as you reasonably can the lower part of the page where -- Dr. Donia, if you will find again what was a little bit confusing was the language basically starts out almost the same. "We don't know much," and if you can find "We don't know much about the Croat delegation."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Okay. It's here on my ELMO anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. This was referred to -- I'm just referring you to something that's in your report. Can you just tell us what that is and is that the -- some of that the language you're referring to when you testified a few moments ago about Karadzic's view toward the Croat delegation at this time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. He expressed this satisfaction with the make-up of the Croatian delegation. "We don't know much about the Croatian -- the Croat delegation, about their skill, but we know they were very much on our side when it came to where sovereignty is primarily realised. They said that sovereignty is to be realised in constituent units and in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina if the constituent units so transfer it." There is then a further elaboration of that on the page we just left, on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Can we now go back to page 2, please. And I'll just leave it to you, sir, if you can direct the courtroom to the language and then read that language.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is toward the bottom of the page. "They are in complete agreement about Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was obvious. Lasic has been eliminated. A delegation which fully shares our views of how Bosnia and Herzegovina should be set up has now arrived." This -- to clarify, Miro Lasic was an active leader in the HDZ who at a meeting on the 29th of January expressed his opposition to cantonisation or territorialisation, and his view, of course, did not prevail in the party, rather the view in support of a territorial division prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much. I think -- I think that will conclude the use of the ELMO for the moment. Thank you very much to the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my questions for now in connection with the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm moving on to another topic unless the Chamber wants to put questions about this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll be working until twenty past twelve and then we'll have our lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if I can now turn your attention for a few minutes to the Muslim party that you've identified earlier today, the SDA or Party of Democratic Action. Once again, can you briefly tell us about the formation of that party.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The SDA was -- or Party of Democratic Action was conceived as a nationalist party of the Bosnian Muslims. Its origins may be found in some meetings that took place between Alija Izetbegovic, who, like Tudjman, was a dissident, who had been imprisoned in socialist Yugoslavia and in fact released only months before the party was formed, and other Bosnian Muslim leaders, including Adil Zulfikarpasic who was living at that time in Switzerland. The meetings resulted in the formulation of a party platform, and the decision to give the party a non-national name, that is the term "Bosnian Muslim" or "Bosniak" does not appear in the name Party of Democratic Action partly because leaders couldn't agree on exactly how to formulate the party's desired constituency in terms of a nomenclature that they would all accept. The party then held its organising or founding convocation in, I believe, May. I may have to check that, 1990, and expressed a platform or articulated a platform which put Bosnian Muslim interests at the heart of the party's objectives and adopted a very ambivalent position about the party's future or Bosnia-Herzegovina's future constitutional relationship to Yugoslavia. It favoured sovereignty for Bosnia-Herzegovina but also asserted its belief that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And this is in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is in 1990, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us any difference, if there was any, between the views of the SDA at this time in terms of how the structure of Bosnia -- I just touched on but I'd like you to go further, please, if you can, how the structure and organisation of the Bosnia-Herzegovina should -- should continue as opposed to what was the view of the Boban faction of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, at this time -- to go back in time a bit to the time of party formation in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Both the SDA and the HDZ had these rather vaguely formulated positions on the constitutional future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Both of them evolved in time, and I've tried in the paper to give you some notion of how those changes took place in response to the changing political environment. By the time that the territorial faction had prevailed within the HDZ, the positions were starkly different between the HDZ and the SDA, the SDA favouring the continuation of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, one which was unified and devoid of these internal divisions which amounted to partition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard, can you tell us, and I mention it now because in connection with the founding Assembly, at that Assembly did Izetbegovic express a view contrary, for example to the banovina concept or plan.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He specifically referred to -- in that address to what he called the shameful Cvetkovic-Macek agreement and said that it should not be repeated in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher's assistance if we have to displace P 09539, able say, Your Honour, at the outset this has not been translated yet. Unfortunately, we found out last night by that oversight a couple of these documents had not been translated, but they are referenced and quoted in parts in Dr. Donia's report. Obviously we'll provide a translation as soon as we can obtain that. If we can have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you refer to in terms of your report, do you cite this document as one that provides an account of Mr. Izetbegovic's statement that the shameful Cvetkovic-Macek agreement to divide this land will not be repeated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. It is on this page of the Sarajevo newspaper Oslobodjenje. I can't read the -- the type.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I can read the Cyrillic. I can't read, I can't see the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's too small?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know whether we can make it larger or not. Will are the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It will be either the second one down the page or the third one down the page. To would -- I think it's probably in the second one. It would take me a few minutes to go through and find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is the article that you're referring to in your paper though?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving ahead, then, from the formation and early history of the SDA -- well, let me just look at my notes for a moment, please. I have no further questions on at that section once again, Mr. President, unless the Judges would like to ask questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on, then, to the elections of November, 1990, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'll just once again ask you, sir, if you can summarise what happened in connection with the November, 1990, elections. How were they conducted and what were the results of those elections?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The elections were held, were generally deemed to be free and fair. There were a few complaints from some of the nationalist parties and, for that matter, some in the opposition, but by and large the voting was perceived by most Bosnians to be open, free, and fair. Defying the predictions of pre-election polls, the three nationalist parties won an overwhelming victory, captured between them or among them the vast majority of seats in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, control of all but two municipal assemblies, and control of all seven positions on the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that these national elections in Bosnia were held in November 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, November 18, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall, sir, or I'll ask for the Chamber's permission for you to refer to your report if you need to, approximately how many seats each of the three nationalists parties won, that is the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, with the Chamber's permission, I will consult it. Yes, Your Honours. The SDA won 86 seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Out of how many?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Out of 240. The SDS won 72, and the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina won 44 seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were there any remaining seats that were taken by other -- various other parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The two leading non-nationalist parties were the Reformists and the Social Democrats. They were the primary recipients of the remaining 38 seats, along with a couple of very small parties that won individual seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I believe you mentioned earlier that as a result of these elections in each of the nationalist parties each won their two seats in the national Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Candidates nominated by the nationalist parties prevailed in each of those categories, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I believe you may have mentioned earlier that when this was originally structured, in addition to the two seats for Serbs, two seats for Croats, and two seats for Muslims, there was also a category or one seventh seat for other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was elected to that position or selected or put in that position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, he was elected. The -- Ejup Ganic, who was a SDA member was elected to that seventh seat. To probably explain that, the SDA ran a candidate for -- in the category of "other," Mr. Ganic, who identified himself as a Yugoslav in the 1981 census, not as a Bosnian Muslim. The SDS ran a candidate as well, the head of the Sarajevo Jewish community, Ivan Ceresnjes, and he did not prevail in the voting for this other category.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as a result of following this election and I believe -- well, I'll ask the next question or two and that will bring us to a breaking point for lunch. Following the results of this election, excuse me, who was selected to be, again, president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic was selected as president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber the process that was involved in that or how that came about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He was elected by the members of the Presidency, but in the background there was an inter-party agreement, an agreement among the three nationalist parties to divide the three leading portfolios in the government among them. The leading vote-getter was to name the president of the Presidency, clearly limited by members of the Presidency, and the head of the -- or president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be selected by the vote-getting party, which turned out to be the SDS, and they selected Momcilo Krajisnik. The president of the government, the position that I know as Prime Minister or Premier, was to be selected by the HDZ. The HDZ selected Jure Pelivan. And each of those positions then was confirmed by a vote in the constitutional bodies that were designated for that role. In other words, the nationalist parties had to support one another in this voting to realise that inter-party agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, then, since the SDA received the largest number of seats, votes, that you mentioned earlier, they then were allowed to, essentially by this inter partes agreement, select Alija Izetbegovic. The Serbs, since they got the second most votes, selected the head of the Assembly which was Krajisnik. And is that the same Krajisnik that's on trial at the Tribunal right now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Just to be clear, the parties made these decisions, not the group as a whole, the political parties, the SDA, SDS, and HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then the HDZ under this arrangement allowed to particular the Premier or Prime Minister who, as you indicated, was Mr. Pelivan. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that brings us to the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, so that we can rest as well as possible, could you tell us how much more time you will need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm proceeding in a completely different way than I had contemplated, I must tell the Chamber, as I think probably is to apparent everyone, and therefore not proceeding nearly at the pace that I had anticipated when I estimated it might be as little as possibly two hours. So I would guess proceeding in the fashion we're now proceeding in it could be -- and, of course, some of the time the Judges quite properly sought to ask questions this morning, I would think, Your Honour, we might -- it might be as long as another hour, hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will break for an hour and a half, and we shall resume around ten to two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.22 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are resuming with our hearing. Please go ahead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will need the usher's assistance, I'm afraid, on the ELMO for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, before we continue on, in light of the procedure we're following, I'd like to take you back to a couple of the exhibits that were referenced in connection with earlier parts of your testimony today, and if you could please look at Exhibit P 08642. If that can please be put on the ELMO. Sir, looking at that page, this is the book from David Owen, Balkan Odyssey. Can you just indicate the reference -- can you just indicate if that page contains the reference in your report to the -- reference to the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement that's quoted in your report in reference to Dr. -- Mr. Owen's statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, on page 36 of Lord Owen's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in a similar fashion if I can ask you -- if I can have the usher's assistance just to hand you or to put on the ELMO P 09537?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the witness said that that was on page 36, and here in this document the pages I have is 35 and 36.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 34 and 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The page reference should be corrected to page 36. Yes, Your Honour. And it will be substituted. The correct page will be provided to you. It was found again -- discovered that when the matter was xeroxed the wrong page was xeroxed. My apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next document that I've asked you to play on the ELMO and again, Your Honours, I said this will have to be addressed pending translation. But also, sir, in reference to the banovina discussion, you made reference to Mate Boban's position. Have you cited this article in your paper concerning a statement by Mr. Boban about the banovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that is Exhibit P 09537. If I can have the usher's assistance, please. I'm now going to hand you part of Exhibit P 00002, page 113 of the book -- of English translation of the book of Franjo Tudjman. If that can be placed on the ELMO, please. If we can possibly zero in as much as possible on the right side of the page, page 113. Sir, you referred to some quotes from President Tudjman's book today in terms of his attitude towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are those statements found on page 113 of his book?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to please put page 114 on the ELMO as well, also from Exhibit P 00002, Franjo Tudjman's book. And on page 114 did you also cite to that quotation from his book, again in connection with his attitude towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think -- and finally, if I can have the usher's assistance, please, to put on the ELMO Exhibit P 08632, page 74. You referenced this morning a statement by Ambassador Zimmermann in his book about statements made to him by Franjo Tudjman. Are some of those statements reflected on this page out of Mr. Zimmermann's book, which is P 08632?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the last document is what number? P what? Because I can't find it in our bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It should be, Your Honour, P 08630, and if it's not on your list, if it's not in the bundle, we will certainly provide it to you. 08630. It is in our bundle, Your Honours. Sorry if there's some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, Dr. Donia, then proceeding forward from where we left off before lunch, I'm going to next direct your attention to several sections of your report taking them somewhat together. It's section 14, Bosnian Serb Parallel Institutions; section 15, Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and section 16, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So to address some of those things in a related way. You mentioned in your testimony earlier today that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established or declared on the 18th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the assistance of the registry, could we display, please, Exhibit P 00302. Looking at that, sir, could you tell the Judges what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is a translation in the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna from September, 1992, of the decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of preparing and conducting your research, did you find -- could you tell the Judges what basis, if any, you found for the apparent reasons why certain municipalities were claimed to be within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The municipalities which are listed in the decision to form the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in my opinion, best correspond to the delineation of territory in the Croatian Banovina of 1939 to '41.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can have the registry's assistance to scroll down that page to where we can see Article 2. I think the Judges will be able to see the municipalities are listed in the document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. And just to be clear, a few of those municipalities are, like the last one, Trebinje Ravno, suggests that part of the municipality is included but not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the same for Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to take your previous answer a bit further, sir, could you tell the Chamber based on your research and work, is there anything that indicates consistently that the municipalities were chosen because in each of these listed municipalities there was a Croat-majority population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I specifically identified Jablanica in my report as having a Muslim majority, and other municipalities on the list also did not have an absolute Croatian majority within their boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you also able to tell whether the election of the municipalities appeared to be based on whether the HDZ had won elections in those municipalities during 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. That didn't seem to be an indicator that that particular municipality would be on the list to the exclusion of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the reasons given in this document for the creation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in your report you indicate that those reasons, or at least some of those reasons, were false. Can you explain that to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The decision cites the -- or makes the allegation that the -- that Bosnia-Herzegovina was not functioning as a state, and therefore the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had to be created. The time -- at the time the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was created, in fact the central institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina were functioning. The members of the HDZ who were elected to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina were actively representing the -- their constituencies in regular meetings of the Assembly, and the central institutions of government were in fact meeting regularly and carrying out their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the registry to scroll so we can see part 1 -- article 1 of the document saying reasons. Just up above on the page. Excuse me. Couple additional questions -- sorry, there is also references -- something -- is there something in this document to be, perhaps in part or reference to, something that happened at Ravno around this time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. It will take me a minute to find it. Yeah. This first few lines of number I, reasons, is apparently a reference to the attack of the Yugoslav national army or Yugoslav People's Army on the village of Ravno just outside Dubrovnik, above Dubrovnik in the municipality of Trebinje, and -- which, as I've indicated in my report, was in fact a horrendous attack and members of that residence, that village, were killed in significant numbers, and the village was ravaged by the Yugoslav People's Army. This appears in the context of November, 1991, to the reference being made in the first paragraph here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But did you understand that event to be an indication that the institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not in fact operating at that time, or functioning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The central institutions were functioning just -- I mean, not just fine, but they were functioning, carrying out their duties at that time. The problem was, of course, that the boundary areas were subject to raids by both Croatian paramilitaries and the Yugoslav People's Army, and on this particular case the ability of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend against such incursions was zero. There were police on the ground, but they were clearly outnumbered and outgunned by the Yugoslav People's Army forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of this Article -- or section I, Article 1, Reasons, in about the fourth line there is the language "The unacceptability of the unitary state model." Can you assist the Judges with what that is an apparent reference to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This was the position of both the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HDZ at this time that Bosnia-Herzegovina could only -- should only continue to exist if it was divided into ethnic enclaves or what was called at the time cantons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving forward, can you tell the Judges in this context or with these things in mind what was -- what had happened during 1991 prior to and around this time in terms of institutions and structures being set up on the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Even before the election of November 18, 1990, Radovan Karadzic announced the creation of a Serbian National Council, which was an institution not within the structure of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in fact a purely Serbian institution. That institution never assumed an active role, but it was the first of several announcements by SDS leaders of separate Serbian institutions to challenge or negate the jurisdiction of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In April, 1991, SDS leaders announced the creation of a community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina in north-western Bosnia, which had that same role but was to consist of a specific territorial unit consisting of the municipalities that declared themselves members of it, and those municipalities with a few exceptions were Serbian-majority municipalities. In subsequent weeks, similar institutions were announced for Herzegovina and for the area around Sarajevo, and in September of 1991, this process took another step forward with the SDS announcing the creation of Serbian autonomous regions or SAOs, as they were known, SAOs. The Serbian autonomous regions, if you looked at them on a map, take up much of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were declared in the course of the second and third week of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the assistance of the registry to switch to display where we can show a PowerPoint slide, I would appreciate it. It is a map that has been provided to everyone in the book of maps that we prepared and given to the Judges and others some days ago. Sir, if you can see that map now, can you briefly describe what that map shows?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It shows the SAOs that were created by number. The one exception here which I think is number 1 was actually styled a little bit differently. It was the I think Serbian region. It had a different title to it in -- in B/C/S, so it was -- it was retitled in September of 1991, in the sense of recognition as its prior status as a community of municipalities. So with that qualification, these are the Serbian -- it's a map of the Serbian autonomous regions that were created in September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So, can I ask you this question then, sir: Did your research show -- are you aware of the fact that some similar institutions or similar parallel organisations were set up on the -- by the HDZ or on the Herceg-Bosna side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Two similar institutions were created in November -- on November 11th, 1991. One was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The other was the Croatian Community of the Bosnian Posavina, which is in the north strip of land in the northern part of the country. On this map it starts just below the word "Croatia" at the very top of the map and goes to the right or east.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's the Posavina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the Posavina, Croatian Community of the Posavina. And the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna being that on -- which is outlined in blue in the lower left-hand part of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, in connection with this map, which for the record I'll just indicate now is Exhibit -- this particular map is Exhibit P 09276. You refer to these as SAOs or abbreviation for Serb autonomous areas. Did you ever in your -- the course of your work here any Herceg-Bosna or HDZ institutions referred to by some similar description?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Commentators in the media immediately started referring to the Croatian communities as HAO, that is the letters for the Croatian autonomous areas, not precisely accurate but many observers noted the fact that the Croatian communities were imitating the similar organisational approach of the SDS in creating these two communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, when you said HAO, it would be H-A-O, H being for Hrvatski, being the Croatian autonomous area. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your work, sir, whether on the Croat side or on the Serb side harks did these parallel institutions if into if you will any sort of plans for either a Greater Serbia or the establishment and carrying out of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The SAOs were a precursor -- or precursors of the creation of a separate institution by the SDS known as the republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was indicated -- there was a meeting in late December which indicated that the SDS planned to create such a republic, and in fact it was pronounced on the 9th of January, 1992. Its constitution was subsequently approved, and on April 7, 1992, the republic of Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared itself independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you -- based on your testimony in a number of what we might call here at the Tribunal in Serb cases, you mentioned several including the Krajisnik case, can you tell the Judges how these Bosnian Serb institutions -- what relationship they had with Belgrade or Serbia and how they were used as part of, if you will, Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, they were supported by the Belgrade leadership and in some sense modelled upon similar institutions that had been created by Serbs in Croatia as early as 1990. As the Serbian republic was formed and started to take actual substance, it received enormous support in the active Serbs within [sic]. It received a great deal of support from the Yugoslav People's Army and political support from the Belgrade leadership in its activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We can leave the map for now, I believe. And going back to Herceg-Bosna, can you tell the Chamber whether any court in Bosnia-Herzegovina found the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to be an illegal organisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued a ruling in September of 1992 declaring the formation of -- known as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to be contrary to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I have the registry's assistance, please, to display Exhibit P 09540. Or forgive me. In the interests of time, let me ask you to please instead display - I'll skip that one - 09541. Can you tell us in reference to your research, sir, what the document indicates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, Your Honour, I will have to provide a translation. The relevant translations are provided in the report, in Dr. Donia's report but not separately from the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not a reference to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hold on. I don't think -- Dr. Donia, I don't think we're getting the broadcast. I think the witness has it but we're not getting the courtroom broadcast as far as I can tell. Okay. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the Constitutional Court members wrote a letter at the time that additional constitutional measures were taken by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and this article refers, I believe, to those measures being taken and the Constitutional Court's letter to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I spelled that out in my paper. It should be distinguished from the ruling of the Constitutional Court which took place in September in 1992, not before that. The reason being that will the Constitutional Court's procedure at that time was to rule on the constitutionality only of those decrees, laws that were published in an official gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did that impact the fact that they issued -- that this Constitutional Court at this time issued some sort of a letter as opposed to a more formal ruling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Again, this is not the document -- the letter is not the document that I'm looking at right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: But in any case, the letter from members of the Constitutional Court was addressed to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and appealed to them to take measures against such separatist acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can I then ask the registry to display Exhibit P 09540. Again, I do not -- again, Your Honours, this one will not be translated apart from the body of Dr. Donia's report. Sir, could you tell us is that reference to the letter you've been telling us in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the practice that was quite common at the time to carry the full text of such pronouncements or correspondence from the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina directed to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could next please go to Exhibit P 00505.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before -- excuse me, Mr. President. Before we go on to the next document, on the previous one where the gentleman indicated this letter, perhaps he can point to us where it's signed, and how does he know that this is the authentic letter? Just for points of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'd like to answer that now, Dr. Donia, you can, although I'm sure Mr. Karnavas will ask you in cross-examination. If you want to address it now, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I'll address it now. As I indicated this is the text of the letter that was carried by the newspaper Oslobodjenje in Sarajevo. It's not the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this the newspaper that at that time was sometimes people talked about newspapers being essentially the paper of record in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can go on to Exhibit P 00505. Can you tell the Judges what this document is. They may have seen it before, I believe, but can you briefly say what that document is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is the text of the Constitutional Court's decision annulling the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and subsequent changes to its statutes and laws that were -- that took place in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges was there subsequently a similar ruling by the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina not on the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna but the subsequent entity called the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask, please, that Exhibit P 08060 be displayed. And can you again, sir, please indicate to the Judges what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Like the previous document, this is a translation of the Official Gazette publication of the Constitutional Court's ruling annulling the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we'll see just by way of summary under "decision," "The decision on the proclamation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in Livno on 24 August 1993 is hereby annulled." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving forward, trying to move as quickly as possible, I'd like to go to another topic. Can you tell the Judges, please, about events leading up to the holding of a referendum in February of 1992 on the question of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the -- from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Toward the end of 1991, the European Community made an effort to systematise its recognition of the states, republics that were seeking independence from Yugoslavia. The EC's involvement goes back some months before that, but -- excuse me. In December, on December 17th, the council of ministers of the EC empowered the commission of jurists known as the Badinter Commission, to accept applications of those republics that wished to achieve recognition as independent from the republics of the former Yugoslavia. Slovenia -- the republics of Slovenia, Croatia and Macedonia applied, and on December 21, 1991, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina over the dissent of its two Serbian members also voted to seek recognition from the EC. The Badinter Commission assessed these applications, and noting the existence of some effort to form a separate Serbian state within Bosnia-Herzegovina, declared that the will of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina to achieve independence was not fully established and therefore recommended that a referendum be held to determine the will of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On January 27, 1992, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted to accept that recommendation and subsequently scheduled a referendum on the proposition of Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence on February 29 and March 1, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. As we continue on the topic of the referendum, can I ask that the registry please display Exhibit P 00116.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I guess we'll have to retrieve a hard copy of the document. Do you have it? Okay. We'll use the e-court I suppose. Thank you. All right. If we can enlarge that a bit, please. Maybe a bit more. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, looking at that document, did you become aware in your research in looking at various documents that there was an HDZ leadership meeting in Grude on the 29th of January of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is -- the document we're looking at is actually a meeting of the leadership of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It obviously consisted of a large number of HDZ leaders, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Briefly, sir, in the interests of time, did you point out two things in this -- in particular, and maybe perhaps others, does this document mention what was happening concerning Mr. Kljuic around this time in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it does. In summary, what this document does is to issue a harsh criticism of the competing wing of the HDZ, that which favoured -- which was opposed to the territorial option or preferred solution whereby Croats throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina would be represented by the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can just interrupt you for a moment, I'm sorry. If we could display page 4 of the document or ERN 00478436. And if we could blow-up or enlarge the bottom of that page. All right. At least in part I think it continues on over to the next page, sir, but just part of the document talking about Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the document, and this is toward the end of the document, essentially blames what's going wrong in the leadership of the party on Mr. Kljuic, and although the -- the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had no formal authority to do so, it recommends an extraordinary meeting of the party which is carried on -- this is in the sentence that begins on this page and carries on to the next page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And it was around that time or shortly subsequent to this time, was it, that Mr. Kljuic was effectively removed from the party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was several days subsequent to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the other topic, and if I can have the registry's assistance to go to page -- page 3 of the document or ERN 00478435. And it's the bottom half of the page approximately. All right. Can you tell us more about what the document says in reference to the referendum and any issues that were being discussed among the Herceg-Bosna leadership at this time about the independence referendum?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Pardon me. There -- I'm getting a little bit confused because there were two meetings at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: One was the 29th of January, which we have in front of us, and the other of which was, I believe, on the 9th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And in this first meeting, which is a Herceg-Bosna meeting, the party essentially announced its intent -- or, I'm sorry, the Herceg-Bosna leadership essentially announced its intent to assume the leadership of the party and criticised the Croatian delegates to -- the Croatian HDZ delegates to the Bosnian Assembly. They also then referred to the desire to amend the language of the referendum and authorised Mr. Boban to -- bestowed upon Mr. Boban the -- the right to determine the timing with which the Croatian people would be informed about the attitude of the party and the HZ HB toward the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In the interests of time, then, if I could direct your attention next to P 00117. If we could enlarge that a bit, please. All right. Sir, will you tell the Judges what this document is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is the record of the session -- the second meeting to which I just referred of the central board or committee of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This meeting was presided over by Mr. Boban, but at that point Mr. Boban was not yet the president of the -- the Bosnia-Herzegovina HDZ. That only took place in, I believe, in September or October of this year. But his presiding over this meeting essentially indicated the drift of the group to revise the language of the referendum and to add a phrase to the referendum, a proposition which stated that the -- that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be divided into cantons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just for the record, say, this was a meeting, and you said "later that year." This is a meeting that took place on the 9th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in that -- does this document go forward and talk about -- and if we could -- excuse me. If we could go forward in that document, page -- the next page, please. In the top part of that page, just to orient everyone in the courtroom to the document, you will see one formulation of a possible referendum. And if you can scroll down that same page, please. So there is the second formula. Can you tell the Judges which of these two formulas were the -- was the formulation, the language that was adopted or approved by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the lower formulation which we're looking at right now was that adopted by the Assembly on January 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It took the language directly from a constitutional amendment to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and only added the word "independent" to that constitutional amendment to formulate the wording of the proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I could ask the assistance for this particular purpose to show -- so we can have a PowerPoint slide, just to put the two specific versions next to each other. Sir, can you point out to the Judges and describe the differences between the two formulations and why -- what is the significance in the different formulations so far as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, there are only two differences. One is that the phrase "other peoples who live in it" has been removed. That is, the formulation in the top version has been removed in the bottom version. And the second, the phrase "in their ethnic areas (cantons)" has been added in the version approved at the meeting of February 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And that was my next question to you. Can you tell the Judges whether this alternative language on the bottom half of this slide, was that approved at the Livno meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was approved at the Livno meetings as the basis for negotiations with representatives of other peoples and parties with the objective of having that adopted for the language of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether that alternative language was ever adopted by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is it correct, sir, that the referendum language that went before the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the end of February was the language in the top part of the page?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the witness to be shown -- well, did the referendum pass?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P 00132. And can you just briefly, sir, tell us, tell the Judges what this document is and what it indicates.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is the translation of the Official Gazette publication of the results of the referendum indicating that about 64 per cent of the registered voters participated and overwhelmingly voted in favour of -- over 99 per cent in favour of the proposition. This also reflects the fact that most Serbs boycotted this vote and therefore did not have their -- their wishes recorded in this proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this vote most -- primarily represents the vote of Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's been previous indication -- well, have you found in your study and in your work -- are you aware of some indications that the HDZ, the Herceg-Bosna leadership pointed to the Croat support of the referendum as some indicated of their support for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, the HDZ leadership supported a yes vote in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But this was not the form of language that they had approved at the Livno meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was not the formal language that they approved at the Livno language and therefore not their preferred formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could you tell the Judges, if the referendum had not passed what would have been the practical result?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The practicality result would have been that Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain a part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we move on to the next and final topic or two, in reference to the same meeting in Livno, a different dimension, do you recall in that meeting whether the issue of Croatian citizenship was discussed, that is that Bosnian Croats be given the right to Croatian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That initiative was presented to the meeting. It was formulated as a request to the Republic of Croatia to include Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina as citizens of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
