utterances.text: Could I ask the registry, please, to go back briefly to Exhibit P 00117. And I believe it is at the -- on page 6, the bottom of page 6 of the translation. And if you can go to the bottom of that page, please. Do you see, sir, the discussion at item number 4?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of the second paragraph that begins with item number 4, could you read the first sentence of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: "The justification for such a demand is that this will be an indestructible thread linking all Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, sir, was this ultimately put into place, and did the Croatian government make provision for Bosnian Croats that is Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be provided Croatian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Moving to another topic, the Cutileiro Plan. Can you tell the Judges what the Cutileiro Plan or the Cutileiro peace process was about and the approximate time that that process was in effect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: With the Badinter Commission having rendered its recommendation that the four republics be recognised as independent, that is Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, and Croatia, the clock began running on the efforts of European Community negotiators to arrive at an agreement that won the support of all three national parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This took place under the aegis of the European Community Committee on Yugoslavia, ECCY, and these talks were held by Jose Cutileiro who was a representative of Portugal which had the rotating Presidency of the European Community. Those talks centred on maps. They centred on efforts by Cutileiro to win the support of all three groups for a -- effectively division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into ethnic cantons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And in the interests of time, can I ask, please, to be displayed the Exhibit P 09546. And can I have the assistance -- thank you. Now, can you tell us what this particular map -- did each -- well, first of all let me ask you. In this process as you've described it as looking at maps, creating maps, did each of the parties, if you will, the principal ethnic parties, the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs, all prepare and circulate proposed maps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did the EC itself or did Mr. Cutileiro then propose his map, if you will?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The situation got rather confused in the hasty course of these negotiations, but in March, indeed Mr. Cutileiro did produce a map and announced that it was -- had been accepted as the basis for further negotiations by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask -- before we talk about this map, could we go to the next page, please. Could you blow that one up, please. Unfortunately, when we blow this up you can't see the title on the top of the page but is this the map proposed by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the areas in white would be the Muslim areas and the areas as we can see on the legend in horizontal lines would be the Croat areas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The areas in white were proposed to be Muslim areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. I misspoke, I'm sorry. If we could go to the next page, please. Before you enlarge that and people see at the top. Is this the HDZ proposed map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go down. All right. I think the map perhaps speaks for itself. And could we go to the next map, please. And this is -- is this the SDS or Serb -- Bosnian Serb map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we enlarge that a bit so. And then if we could go back to the first page of the exhibit. And was this then having received and considered these, the three maps presented by each of the parties, is this the map that the EC proposed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, please, did the Cutileiro process ever result in any sort -- either an agreed map or any other agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, it did not. The objections of the various parties were really voiced only after the initial announcement by the EC that this whole thing had been accepted, but in fact there were profound difficulties from the beginning, and it's apparent that the parties never concurred on this map or any other nor on the principles that were proposed by Mr. -- the constitutional principles that were proposed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, moving on to another section of your report which talks about the Croatian Defence Council or HVO. Because of time I'm only going to ask you a couple of questions. Can you -- at one point on page 36 of your report -- sorry. In the second paragraph of that report and it's the only way I know -- I'm asking for specific clarification of the language you've used, so I -- you say the Presidency -- in the second paragraph, the Presidency of the HZ HB? What are you referring to when you say the Presidency, because today we've heard at that Presidency can be used to mean a number of different things.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I -- without looking at my reference in the report, I really can't give a clear answer, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with Your Honour's permission, may Dr. Donia look at report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. If we could have just a neutral answer to that question, what does Presidency mean? The president, the Presidency, these are sort just sort of neutral, and then he can look to see in what context it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's the problem, Your Honour, it means different things in different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I dare so no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not here to have Mr. Karnavas testify either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How would you define the word "Presidency"? What to your mind is "Presidency"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it can mean either a single individual who was the president of a body or a collective group of people who share and divide the responsibility of that position of typically head of state. I should add that there -- every -- about every body you can identify at this time was creating presidencies and having arguments about who was the president of the Presidency. So these were very commonplace discussions and had a little bit different meaning in each context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, when you would refer to -- Your Honour, with your indulgence, again I'm looking at paragraph 2 of pair 36, when you in that part of your report refer to the Presidency of the HZ HB, what body or person are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the HZ HB in fact created a collective Presidency when it was formed, and my reference here is to that collective body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also in your report in various places use the terminology the HVO and then separate word or abbreviation, HZ HB. What does that reference mean or refer to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Again, without looking at the report I can't -- I can't really answer that -- that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I would ask the Court to allow to direct Mr. -- Dr. Donia's attention to the end of paragraph 1 and page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before doing so, Your Honour, I would like to know whether Dr. Donia, after all these years, knows what the HVO means. Is there more than one meaning? If so, we would like to have those. And also, if he knows what it means, HZ HB. And he can give us the meaning. I think after all these years, you know, when he first testified in Blaskic, he should know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will break it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a question that the Judges would like to have a answer to. What do you consider the HVO to be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO was an organisation created to fuse military, civilian, and administrative leadership within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P 00152.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what that document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is the English translation of the declaration published in the Official Gazette to form the HVO or the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the date of this document, sir, if we can see it. It may be --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Like many of these documents, it was published in September, 1992, but pertains to an earlier proclamation or decision reached on April 8, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, around this same time, if I can ask you -- excuse me, the registry's assistance to direct your attention to P 09543.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, Your Honour, I'll have to tender this marked for identification pending translation because it's again quoted and interpreted in the body of the report but not -- there is not a separate translation at this particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what happened around this time in connection with the Bosnian government forming a military arm -- or an armed force for the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That is newspaper of April 16, 1992, and the headline halfway down the page on the right-hand -- right three columns says: "All formations under the command of the Territorial Defence." This was the announcement by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina that all armed formations in the country should come under the command of the Territorial Defence forces central command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did that include at that time any reference either then or later to including the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know. That's -- I'm not certain. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that if we have time. But around the same time, sir, you were saying -- I'm sorry, can you give us the date of this again, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The newspaper is dated April 16, 1992, and pertained to an event that was -- or announcement made, proclamation of April 15, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Donia, if we can move on to what I think would be then our final topic. Can you tell the Judges -- sometimes something's referred to as the Graz Agreement. Can you describe what that was and the circumstances surrounding that to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In early May of 1992, Mate Boban and Radovan Karadzic met in the Austrian city of Graz to work out a territorial division of Bosnia-Herzegovina which they styled as a peace agreement. It was done without the participation and apparently without the knowledge of any Bosnian Muslim leaders. They did arrive at an agreement which, except for territory near Mostar along the Neretva River, represented that division which included a small territory allocated to Bosnian Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Could I ask that the registry please display Exhibit P 00187. Could I ask you to go -- there's several pages of this. Could I ask you to go to the previous page, perhaps. Or do you have the previous page? Thank you very much. And just focusing on that top part of the page. You stated a moment ago that this purported to be some sort of a peace agreement. You'd indicated in your answer a moment ago, you said there appeared to be an agreement except for some territory near Mostar along the Neretva River. Now, if we could go back to the exhibit and is that -- is that disagreement reflected in items number 1 and 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Points 1 and 2 spell out that difference in views.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the -- well, sorry, before we get to that, can we next look at Exhibit P 00192. And part of that -- I'm sorry, may I have -- if you would go down several pages into that document, please. It could be about the third page of that document. And please continue on down. ERN 00332081. Page 4, I'm told, of that particular exhibit. I'll ask the usher to please display on the ELMO this part of the exhibit. Still in reference to Exhibit 192 but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's a question that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to, and it's probably a question to the Prosecution. We have this 192 document, and the English version looks like a photocopy of a photocopy of a photocopy perhaps, whereas the B/C/S version looks freshly typed on a computer. Now, what is the explanation? Did they -- did they issue a document in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Subject to being corrected, Your Honour, because I don't want to be accused of testifying, but it's my understanding that, yes, because this document -- part of the document was issued for the purposes of the -- for the consumption of the international community there was an English version prepared, and I'm sure -- and I -- well, I shouldn't say I'm sure. I'm pretty confident that the reason the B/C/S translation looks crisp by comparison is that in this particular instance the B/C/S translation has been prepared at the ICTY of the English document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, looking -- I guess I don't have the ELMO display. Sorry. Can you just explain, in your report you talk about the fact that there was the perception or the position that was taken that the effect of the Graz Agreement was in fact to undo or overturn the referendum on independence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That -- pardon me. That's the assertion made in this press release of Ian Greer and associates which was the public relations agency employed by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you point to the Judges, please, refer them to the language that you're referring to now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph. "The agreement overturns the mandate of the Bosnian independence referendum for self-determination for a Bosnian state. Instead, the mandate will be reversed. Bosnia will be divided and in its place three separate states will be formed."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell the Judges whether this agreement was ever recognised by the international community or carried into effect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. In fact, evoked a rapid and rather angry response from EC negotiators that no agreement could be reached without the participation of all three parties, and they declined to accept the offer made by Boban and Karadzic to arbitrate their differences in the Neretva valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you also then finally, sir -- to your knowledge did any representative of the Muslim ethnic group, if you will -- was there any Muslim participation in the negotiation leading to this Graz Agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of the witness. I will tender the exhibits at the appropriate time, whenever you wish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, that completes the examination-in-chief. It is time to take a break anyway. Fifteen seconds for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since you said yesterday that I would be the first to cross-examine based on the rotation, I would just like to inform you that the Defence counsel have reached an agreement about how to conduct today's cross-examination and will be proceeding in the following way: All the Defence counsel and Defence teams have delegated their entire time to the Defence of Jadranko Prlic and the Defence of Valentin Coric. That means Mr. Karnavas and my learned friend Mr. Jonjic will be conducting the cross-examination, and they have reached an agreement between themselves as to how to divide the time. In addition to this, if there is sufficient time left over from the time you have allotted to us, the Defence of General Petkovic and Bruno Stojic principally, possibly some others as well, might be asking one or two brief questions or seek clarification, nothing more than, but let me repeat, only if we have surplus time. Which I don't suspect we will. The third point I wanted to raise is this: We will in all events stay within the frameworks of the time allotted to us. However, with respect to the time now, looking at the clock, I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber to tell us how much time we're going to have and to make a short story of it before you ask the question, it seems to be 20 minutes past three now. The Prosecution had two hours for cross-examination. They said they would take two hours, but they have taken more, double, almost double the time that the Prosecution had announced, the initial two hours, and so bearing in mind the principle that guided us with previous witnesses, the Defence expects, first of all, to be given at least as much time, because it is quite obvious that this overstepping of time by the Prosecution cannot be to the detriment and disadvantage of the Defence. And as you have already intimated, we would just have until the end of business tomorrow, the end of day tomorrow, which means that part of the time from our fund has already been used up by the Prosecutor. So regardless of the fact when we have to complete our cross-examination, because we, according to this schedule would be moving into Monday, regardless of the calendar days, we consider that we should be given at least as much time as was taken up effectively by the Prosecutor today. I think that that was all that I had to tell you. We, of course, are at your disposal if you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. So the legal assistant officer has said that the Prosecutor used three hours and 31 minutes. Now, in respect to what was announced yesterday, they had an extra one and a half hours. So as of now, the Defence, up until tomorrow, will have in actual fact five and a half hours, because we're going to have an hour and a half now left over for us, plus the four hours of tomorrow, which makes five and a half hours in total. Which means that the Defence, according to that calculation, will have two hours more than the Prosecution had. So that is food for thought. Think about the problem. But a priori, you're going to have two extra hours, two more hours than the Prosecution. So you can divide this time up amongst yourselves, and we ought to finish tomorrow at 1.45. We'll discuss the matter later on, but it is 3.20 now, and we'll reconvene at 3.40. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to Mr. Karnavas, just one point I'd like to specify. Mr. Scott, the exhibits which you listed earlier today, you would like these exhibits to be tendered into evidence or are you waiting for the end of the cross-examination before asking these to be tendered into evidence? So what's your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to tender them now. I was just trying to be sensitive to the time situation, but I'm happy to tender them at this time. I believe they should be Exhibits -- I'm not going to -- unless the registry needs me to I won't refer to all the 0's, but 2, 13, 31, 89, 116, 117, 132, 152, 187, 192, 302, 505, 1043, 8060, 8630, Your Honour, marked for identification pending translation, 8632, again marked for identification subject to translation, 9356 [sic], 9537 pending translation, 9538, 9539 pending translation, 9540 pending translation, 9541 pending translation, 9542 pending translation, 9543 pending translation, 9544, again pending translation, and 9546 for the four maps, and 9547, also pending translation. And I may have -- also, Your Honour, 9 -- sorry, I don't know if it's on here or not. Also, 9276, which was the one map of the Serbian autonomous areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. There has been probably a slip of the tongue. When you mentioned 5956 you probably had in mind -- you said 9596 and you referred to probably 9536. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, absolutely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the list of exhibits is concerned, there are a number of exhibits pending translation. So the registrar will give a -- will mark these exhibits for identification. There is one exhibit which we still need to rule upon; we shall confer after the hearing, which is the expert's report, number P 9536. So we shall wait for the end of the cross-examination and let you know what we do about it. But the other documents which you mentioned of various origins are documents which can currently be tendered into evidence. Registrar, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The following documents are therefore admitted -- tendered -- sorry, admitted today: Dukes P 0002, P 0013, P 0031, P 00089, P 00116, P 00117, P 00132, P 00152, P 00187, P 00192, P 00302, P 00505, P 01043, P 08060, P 9356, P 09356, P 09538, and P 09276. And as per the decision of the Chamber the following documents are only marked for identification which they remain as marked for identification, and these are the reference: P 08630, P 08632, P 09537, P 09539, P 09540 [Realtime transcript read in error "P 0940"], P 09541, P 09542, P 09543, P 09544, and P 09547. These are marked for identification until a translation is provided to the registry. Finally, the report of the expert witness P 09536 is -- will be admitted only after -- well, pursuant to your decision, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be schoolmaster again, but I think instead of P 095 -- 0940 you wanted to say 09540. It's on line 8. The second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't want to take any time but the only confusion I still have left, at least from mine, it may only be me, at line -- on page 106, line 4, there's reference to P 9356 and then P 09356, and again we have 9536 which is the report, but I don't think we had a 9356. Could it possibly have been 9276?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. The expert witness report is number 9536, subject to our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now give the floor to Mr. Karnavas. And over the break we discussed this very briefly. We have decided to grant the Defence team two extra hours, two more hours than the Prosecution. That said, the Defence teams will be entitled to call their own historical witness, so you will plenty of time to make additional comments by calling your own witnesses. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to condense a four-day cross-examination into four or five hours. It will be a challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I trust you are okay to continue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And by the way, congratulation on your new book that just came out on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't by any chance bring a copy for us to look over during the evening in case I wanted to, you know, as you a couple of questions on it tomorrow since you go all the way to 2003?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'll wait for you to buy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, well, my question is, do you have it here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I do not have a copy here, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't bring one for the Prosecutor to look at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he didn't ask for one either, as I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He's also waiting for me to buy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's market economy as opposed to the command economy back in the days of the former Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, right. Now, a little bit about your qualifications. You touched on it today. We have your CV, but let's just get right to it. You got a Ph.D. from the University of Michigan; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And because we speak the same language, we're going to have to pause a little bit. Yesterday, I was -- it was rather challenging for folks in the translation booth. My fault. That was a rather specialised the Ph.D. dissertation that you did; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you could just share the period, the time period within which that dissertation evolved.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: You mean the time that covered, the historical period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, the period that it covered.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It covered the period 1878 to 1914.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1878 to 1914. That's in Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it dealt with the Muslims of Bosnia during that period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It didn't cover earlier periods, some periods which we might find in your report or which you testified earlier or which you wrote in another book with your -- with your mentor; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct. It did not address periods before 1878.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it didn't cover periods afterwards because you stopped right there, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So the period that we're talking about prior to World War II, during World War II, after World War II, the break-up of Yugoslavia, none of that is covered in your report; right -- in your dissertation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it when you do a dissertation you really focus into the area; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Most dissertations are very specifically defined by area, by chronological period, and by topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And you have a mentor that walks you -- that helps you along the process? Or maybe even more than one?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the reason for having a mentor is to make sure that the research is done properly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That you cite the sources that you need to cite and they're cited properly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, not taken out of context. That's one of the -- I mean, among other things.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Making sure that you read the proper sources. In other words, you have got to look through them before you begin to discriminate which you're going to use and which you're going to discard for whatever reasons; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. The mentor in general helps formulate the research strategy which includes literature and the exploration of archival sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it's a rather tedious process, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It certainly is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that dissertation, I bet, is heavily footnoted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It -- it is significantly footnoted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, if one were to go to the footnote and check out whatever it is in the footnote, it would exactly say, you know, what it purports to say, you know, what it's being cited for in other words?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it, just one last question on that -- on this issue, I take it through this entire process you learn a methodology about doing research and writing on a particular topic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that methodology is the same methodology that you could use for future purposes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: One could use that methodology for future purposes, but I would say there's not a single methodology which is used in all historical writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And not, for that matter, in all dissertations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There are different methods?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Different methods, different approaches to presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And also different groups of historians; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course if all depends on which group you fit in. It may depend on the outcome of -- of the historical conclusions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to touch on that a little bit later, but just to highlight this portion, reasonable historians can reasonably disagree. You've heard that phrase before here in The Hague. And, by the way, just in case you need anything, I've gone ahead and read through all your transcripts. I have them over here. But you've -- you've acknowledged that; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: My sympathies to you for having read through the transcripts, but I have certainly knowledge and acknowledged now that historians frequently have disagreements on interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On interpretations of the same events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on the same data that they look at; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Although some may exclude certain data or decide not to use it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Some may place more focus on certain data as opposed to other data?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That's a function of the way the topic is formulated and also of the method of exposition to be used in the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, since your dissertation you wrote a book. I believe that was in 1994, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was while all hell was breaking loose in the former Yugoslavia, specifically in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time, you were still employed for Merrill Lynch?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for those of us who aren't -- who don't know who Merrill Lynch is or aren't fortunate enough to be able to invest in Merrill Lynch, what is it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Merrill Lynch is a large diversified financial services firm with global operations but based in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And after getting your dissertation, as I understand you taught four years and thereafter you went to work for Merrill Lynch?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Rather different. You know, big switch I would say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And is it fair to say that some of the tools that you learned while you were doing your dissertation were not necessarily being applied while you were working at Merrill Lynch?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Some of the tools were not, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I mean, of course you learn how to use logic and common sense and that sort of stuff, analyse documents and those sorts of things you could always use; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you weren't doing sort of like risk assessments of certain countries or regions such as, you know, to see whether investors should invest in a particular region or country like the former Yugoslavia that would give you some of the edge, the inside knowledge of what was happening in that region?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So it would be fair to say and by -- and you can correct me any time you want, but it would be fair to say that during that period, for all intents and purposes you were focusing in your new occupation, your new job, right, your new vocation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Principally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And history had become an avocation at that point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as part of your avocation you occasionally would do a book review; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And might we say that your 1994 book that you did was slightly more than just a avocation but not necessarily what one would consider a scholarly work?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I would not share that characterisation. I think it was a work using scholarly methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And designed for a more general audience than the typical scholarly work addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I think we partly address. You know, using a scholarly methodology ask not the same thing as producing a scholarly, you know, text?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And by that I mean is -- what I mean is, for instance, when you look at the book, and I have -- I have read it -- by the way, I have purchased it, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That when I look at it, a lot of footnotes are missing. I mean, one would expect, because you're making a bold statement, and I would look to see -- and I would find no footnote. Would you agree with me on many instances that is the case in your book?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we set out to minimise the scholarly apparatus in terms of extensive footnotes and lengthy bibliography.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, would you not, that if someone who has a footnote fetish like me who would want to actually go and look at the footnote and actually kind of check it out and make sure that what you're citing is indeed you know relevant and pertinent, I wouldn't be able to do that with your work? And I'm not trying to diminish it, but I'm just saying I wouldn't be able to check out exactly to see whether what you're claiming is indeed factually based on data.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, being, let's say, brief on scholarly apparatus, it was indeed -- it contained many things which were based on general assertions and understanding and therefore are not footnoted. So if you have that fetish, it probably would be difficult to find support for some of the propositions made in the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I just want to make sure you said general assertions. You would agree there's a lot of general assertions that you're making in that particular text; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I indicated that it came out in 1994. You were still working for Merrill Lynch. I take it full time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Pretty demanding job?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Especially, as I understand, you were at a supervisory level so you had to make sure -- under the principle of command responsibility, you had to make sure that the folks beneath you were doing their job; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so -- but during that period of time, you found the time to write a book with your mentor, and I take it you must have had -- had to go to Sarajevo or to Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to do some original research?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. The book was specifically committed to an account which was not based on extensive original research but on available sources from other works, Radio Free Europe reports. This was real little at a time when those documents were extremely difficult to come by in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you caught my attention here when you say extensive. "Not based on extensive original research." Now, that would lead me to believe that you did some original research. Maybe not extensive but some?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Might you be so kind as to tell us what original research you did?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I went through the -- I just mentioned Radio Free Europe reports, which were continuous through the 1980s and early 1990s. I also looked into some of the documentation pertaining to the earlier periods in which we -- we dealt. For example, the census reports which gave a history of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its ethnic composition. There are a number of other things, but I would cite those as significant among the things that I looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But those are secondly sources; right? They're not original research?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I would say the census reports are -- qualify as primary source. I think the distinction between a primary source and a secondary source is often difficult to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But first, I have a technical problem here, Your Honour. If I may indulge for one second and try to fix it. I apologise to everyone. Okay. We're back on line. All right. I don't know what I touched, but it went off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, all right. We're talking about your book. Did you -- and we left off on primary and secondary. What would you consider to be primary sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the usual definition is a document that is generated by a direct participant in an event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It's, as I say, a rather fuzzy, flexible, if you will, definition. Many primary sources may exist in an archive somewhere but are then published word for word in a collection and are also then normally considered primary sources. Secondly sources, therefore, are the works of other scholars who have examined particular issues or particular sources and written their conclusions based on their examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could just deal with the primary sources. You talked about, I guess, actors, we could call them, folks that participated in the events. For your 1994 book, I mean some of the actors, if you were in Sarajevo, did you speak with Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was available at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I never went to Sarajevo prior to the public -- completing the writing of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the book was written from afar?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So would it be fair to say for at least that particular book you didn't have any interviews, face-to-face, tete-a-tete?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't recall that I had any interviews for that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But based on the collection of the documents that you were able to get, you were able to draw some general conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to switch over here at the ICTY. You indicated that this is your eighth time that you're testifying; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would it be fair to say that the first time that you testified was the first time that you testified anywhere as an expert?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At least in this kind of a setting; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: First time, period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. First time, period. And so one might say that being a novice at the time, you might not have known what exactly your task would be as an expert?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that I was a novice at the time, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You just said that you hadn't testified before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: If you mean that I was a novice as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I would accept that characterisation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. So you were a novice. I take it they had to walk you through what you needed to do in order to prepare?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They gave me a charge --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- which I then attempted to execute, and the testimony was the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. They gave you a charge. Now, when you say "a charge," does that mean they gave you the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They gave me the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's stop here and, you know, let's park a little bit and try to figure this one out. And help me out here. The indictment usually tells a story, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Part of it does typically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And might we say that it tells the Prosecution story?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I mean, it, the Prosecution, alleges X, Y, and Z and sort of, at least in the Prosecution's mind, rightly or wrongly, they formed an opinion; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They believe that the person that they're indicting, that person is indeed guilty and they can prove that beyond a reasonable doubt; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So it would be fair to say that when you came in at least at the very first time, and of course this applies for all the other times, but at least for the very first time when you came in, they didn't say here -- here is some material, look it over, and if you need anything else, let us know, and come up with an expert report? They didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. In fact, as I understand it in, in the Blaskic case you didn't produce a report but you had some notes that you were making reference to, that you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I had a 19-page outline --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- that I referred to in the course of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: But no written text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. In fact, during the case, during the trial, one of the Defence lawyers asked for that outline because it hadn't been provided; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But he probably you let you look at it more than I did today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: About the same, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you then testified in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, try and speak more slowly because perhaps the interpreters are having a little trouble following you, if you could. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again I apologise to the interpreters. I just had a coffee and that excites me a little bit, but I'll try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The next time you testified was in Kordic; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By this point you were no longer a novice. You had at least gone through the right of passage; you'd testified, so you kind of knew what it was to be an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in that case, it's deal with the Muslim-Croat conflict, it was -- the issues were relatively identical or the same or similar?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Similar, yes, uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in that case you did in fact produce a report, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But in that case there were no footnotes, were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There was no scholarly apparatus to the report except for a few quotations which were cited in the course of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, a report doesn't need to necessarily be scholarly in order to have footnotes. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- but in other words, in the report itself, you were making assertions and there was no way to know where exactly those assertions were coming from or at least how you had come to certain conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Some of the conclusions were backed by quotations that were included in the text of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The report, of course, began very, very early in time and covered a long historical period and ended up with the contemporary period just up to April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But it did not have sources from which the lawyers could look at some of the assertions that you were making in order to see whether the assertions were well-founded based on historical facts or historical data that could be tested.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Some of those assertions were backed up by sources that were cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Those are the quotations; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm talking about other, because you said it was a long report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I was not asked to -- I was asked not to footnote that report, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Really? The Prosecutor actually told you don't footnote?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked me to essentially replicate the historical account that I had given verbally in Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that Mr. Nice that did that? I mean we don't want to out them out, but I'd like to know who was --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't recall who gave me that charge initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you would agree with me though for the Defence lawyer it would be very difficult to go and check the assertions that you are making unless there were footnotes there for them to check; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They didn't seem to have any difficulty doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you didn't answer my question, though, did you? It would appear, though, that without foot notes one would have a difficult time checking your assertions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take that. We're late in the game. All right. Now, that issue, though, did come up during the trial, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, the lawyer walked you through it. It was a very interesting cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, uh-huh. It was interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And he pointed out how you not only had no footnotes but there was no peer review of that report; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And at least at the end of that rather interesting cross-examination, you at least must have felt that at least for the next time you would know what to do should you be called upon to do a report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I certainly felt --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Uneasy.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- the next time that I came to address one of these things that more scholarly apparatus would be appropriate --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- and continued to hold that view. It was, I think, the judgement of the -- the Prosecutor that that was in a sense an obstacle to a straightforward understanding why the Court -- of the basic historical chronicle that was laid out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Prosecutor thought that the Trial Chamber, the Honourable Members of the Trial Chamber weren't able of understanding the report if it had footnotes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, that's not the statement that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, help me out here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think the Prosecutors felt it was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: A barrier to impeded effective communication of what was a fairly basic historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Since then, you've produced reports with footnotes and obviously the Judges haven't been impeded by those foot notes have they? To your knowledge, at least?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were once asked and I believe it was the Stakic case. I have it here. I can pull it out if you want me to, but you were asked whether at least in that particular case if it was important for you to do comprehensive reports if -- if and when you're called upon to testify in cases of this magnitude. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You recall being asked whether your report was comprehensive?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you don't recall your answer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you this before I get to it: Would you agree that with a case such as the crimes that are being tried over here, the crimes alleged, do you think it's important for someone like yourself, an expert, to be rather comprehensive when coming in here and producing a report for the Trial Chamber's assistance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think it depends on how the charge to me is formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It -- to be truly comprehensive gets one into hundreds of pages, perhaps even multiple volumes, and I don't think that's the purpose of my testimony or my report, either in this case or in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you say that your report is comprehensive, the one that you've produced?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you say that you've looked at all the alternative plausible or alternative sources that are out there that might hold a different point of view that you would?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you think, do you think, and help me out here, but do you think it would be important for the honourable members of our Trial Chamber to have that information so at least you could say, well, here's what I looked at. Here's what I agree with. Here's what I don't agree with. Here's how I came up with my conclusion, and here is why. Do you think that might be important?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think that would be up to the Honourable Judges to decide. My own purpose is, let's say, more restricted than that. It is to provide a narrative account which can in fact be challenged and alternative interpretations presented, but again I do not want to run into 200 pages or multiple volumes for the purpose of a historical background --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. Do you think it would be important for the Trial Chamber to have a comprehensive report from an historian such as yourself if indeed that is what you're coming here to testify about, the historical facts and drawing conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that is a piece of literature which is available in printed version and by many authors, and far beyond the scope of what I set out to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, we'll talk about that in due course. But let me ask you this. In this case as in the other cases, did the Prosecution provide you with the indictment before they gave you your task?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Rather comprehensive one, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it they gave you the amended version as well? It got even longer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you read it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Read it carefully?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by the time you got through reading it, you fully understood what exactly the Prosecution's position was? Hard to miss it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: On the questions addressed, I would say, yes, I had a very good understanding of the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and again, in this particular case they didn't come to you and say, Mr. Donia or Dr. Donia, you're the expert. You're the historian. Obviously you would know what documents I need to look at. You would need -- that you need to look at. You would know who to talk to, the primary, the secondary sources. Okay. They didn't say to you, you choose it. You choose the list and we'll provide it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. That was not the charge I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And did they say to you by any chance, well, if you need anything you let us know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it by saying that they must have given you something first; right? What they believe you needed; right? What they believe you needed to do this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- in fact, inquired about the availability of certain documents in the Office of the Prosecutor and asked that they be provided if they had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how many documents would you say --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I asked specifically for the party platforms, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: HDZ, and SDA. All together, perhaps, I don't know, 25 documents that I had not investigated before that have come available on particular topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did they provide you with a list of documents to start with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So they just told you here, what do you need, and that's the list that you asked for?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you by any chance ask for an index so that you would know what documents they might have? Because after all, let me clue you in, the Prosecution has been going around the former Yugoslavia having access to various archives. All right? Did you ask, by any chance, could I look at the list of documents from the various archives, be they from the BiH, be they from Croatia, and so on and so forth? Did you ever ask for that list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. Life is too short to look over that list in one of the archives alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I agree with you on that one. But I guess if we're going to be looking at crimes of this nature, and we're going to be looking at trying to ascribe responsibility for certain events, and if we're trying to make historical sense, wouldn't you think it would be important to look at all the documents from all the sides so you can put the events into context and try to make sense of them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, that was not my charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask whether that was your charge. I'm asking you if you think it was important.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I believe it's important for this Court to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you ask for -- to see the list of material that they have? Yes? No?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know that they had a list that you could have looked at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I -- I can't say I knew or know that there is a single list of available documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did they share with you by any chance the list of documents that they thought might be important for this Trial Chamber to review?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, help me out here. Maybe I'm just -- maybe I'm -- I'm making it too complex, but you're here because you're supposed to be an expert; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you have a particular expertise and that would be history; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Never mind that your dissertation was for a different period, different events. Nonetheless, we've established that you have the methodological tools to conduct the research. Would it be fair to say that they should be coming to you and asking you what information you need, what documentation you need, which witnesses you might wish to interview in order for you to -- to prepare a comprehensive report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. As I've indicated, they did not ask me to prepare a comprehensive report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They asked me to prepare a report which dealt with a specific period which ended in approximately the fall of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And did not go directly to the key issues of responsibility that are before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I've noticed in -- by the way, it may sound like I'm being critical. I'm not, but I think it would be fair to say that if I came to you as the expert, you would be telling me what you need. I mean, if I tell you this is what I'm looking for, you would be the one to tell me, Oh, I need this document, I need to do this and that and the other, because you're the expert, I'm not. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Generally speaking. Sometimes I know what to ask for and sometimes I don't know what to ask for in terms of the corpus of documentation that -- that's available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated in your report -- let me see over here. I'm cutting parts of my cross so we can move along. But this is sort of like -- you say encylopaedia-like entries. That kind of caught my attention. What does that mean? Encylopaedia-like entries. Are they stand-alone chapters that one could look at and that encylopaedia-like entry would be comprehensive in and of itself? Might that be what you're suggesting here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think I'm suggesting that they are stand-alone entries that deal with the kind of essential irrelevant reducible facts and -- and the positioning of the institutions and events that I've examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I would again say my purpose here is not to be comprehensive. It is, in fact, to be synthetic, to be as much a provider of a digested, abbreviated account of each of these topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Sort of like the Reader's Digest version of the events.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: USA Today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: USA Today versus New York Times or Le Monde?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right, okay. But the stand alone chapters they're not comprehensive in the sense that you would have looked at all necessary documents for this little stand-alone chapter or section to be balanced and objective?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I have not -- not only have I not looked at all documents, I have not looked at the total corpus of scholarly production on these individual sections. They're all topics which are much broader and more extensive and on which there is a large corpus of scholarly work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: More so than I would be able to develop a command of for each of these sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be fair to say that in this condensed, synthesised mode these stand-alone chapters, while they may be informative, may not necessarily be quite as accurate as we may want them to be, at least for this particular setting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I would say my goal was to make them as accurate as possible, and I think I've achieved that in important ways, also confident that there will be statements in there that are, first of all, subject to being contested, and second, there may be an error. I mean, there -- it's possible. But this is my best effort to prevent -- to present that compact synthesised version of the institutions, events, and leading actors concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and before I go on to that, the issue was whether it would be accurate. You're trying -- in your report, in these entries encyclopaedia-like which are supposed to be stand alone because you tell us that, we can jump around from subject to subject if we wish, you, in fact, did not look at relevant information from all sides; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think it depends on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So some topics are more comprehensively treated than others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Not necessarily comprehensively treated but there are certain topics about which I have a priori knowledge of some of the documentary base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Some topics on which I've written before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: So the challenge is to condense and become succinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And other topics on which it would be utterly impossible to cover the full spectrum of source information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I have a burning question that you might be able to answer. If you haven't looked at certain documents, if you haven't looked at certain archives that maybe out there that may contain -- in fact, I would I submit do in fact contain valuable information, how on earth would you know what to discriminate, what is good what is bad, if you haven't taken the time to look at it or hasn't been provided to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, as a general question, I think the answer is you have defined the bane of the historian's existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: One can expend lifetime and more on a very narrow topic and never truly have examined everything that is there or that is coming out, and so the report is in its individual sections an effort to capture the -- the essence of these issues and institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, I know that they gave you a cut-off period. Did -- did they select the topics or was this something that you selected and ran it by them, and after, you know, the Prosecutor acting like the editor, for instance, for a publication, they would okay go with these or add some more? How did they --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I was -- I was charged to keep it brief, to keep it encyclopaedic, if you will, and to work on specific topics. I then ran those topics past the Prosecution and was asked to address a couple others and added those then to the report. So I would say it was kind of a mutual process of identifying the topics to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it would be fair to say that by looking at these topics you could not get a -- a comprehensive or a complete picture of the events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, to take one example, the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is an absolutely enormous, huge task. Thousands of books have been produced on this, and I wouldn't in any sense pretend that that section is comprehensive or takes into account all the existing scholarly literature or documentation. So the answer in that -- in that case is certainly this is not a comprehensive or complete picture of events, because it's got to be short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But on at that particular topic, for example, since you mentioned it, is it not fair that there are many scholars in your field that disagree with you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the sense -- yeah. And they hold different opinions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So what you provided us here today is just one, you know, plausible historical explanation and there may be other plausible historical explanations; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that would go also along the line of some of the other topics that you talked about today, no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in preparing this particular report, did you have any tete-a-tete interviews, in other words, with primary sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I routinely talked to a lot of people about their opinions and understanding of things and occasionally do a formal interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: But I did not do any formal interviews specifically in preparation for this report. I certainly benefited from the general discussions that I've had over the years with various people and expect that that may be reflected in some of the things that I said without being specifically based on an individual interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've indicated that this is your eighth time testifying. I believe Blaskic was in 1997. Your first book was in 1994. From the -- from that period, 1997, say, until 2000 -- what are we in 6, 2006, did you interview any of the major actors in this story? And I'll name a few, by the way.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I have interviewed some of the -- a few of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- actors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you interview the late President Tudjman when he was alive to find out what exactly he meant when he wrote X, Y, and Z in his particular texts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you make an attempt to interview him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the Office of the Prosecution forbid you from trying to interview President Tudjman, you know, because otherwise you're trying to delve into his mind, trying to figure out what on earth man was thinking at a particular time in history in the context of the events; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. At some point in time you're trying to assess what were the motives of the late President Tudjman at a particular historical event; right? That's one of the things you're trying to achieve?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it might have been good, might it not, to have perhaps sought an interview with the late President Tudjman? As I understand, he was a pretty open guy, welcomed reporters, welcomed historians, he was an historian himself. Did you ever try to interview him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution tell you stay away from Tudjman, don't interview him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did they ever forbid you from interviewing anybody you wanted to interview?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you could have interviewed, for instance, Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Price to his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Prior to his deaths. Of course, he's no longer with us. Susak?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
