utterances.text: If we're going to talk about some of the reports that you prepared for earlier cases and some of the issues that you opined on, might we not say that there were actors out there available for you to interview and you chose not to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did notice somewhere, I believe it was in the Kordic case, I think it was the Kordic case but it might be the Blaskic, where you did take rather some pride in saying that you interviewed Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I stated that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know that I was bragging about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you weren't bragging. I'm sort of making light of the matter, but you were asked if you met -- if you had conducted any interviews or looked at any primary sources and you said, well, yes, Kljuic. But then you stopped right there. It was full stop. Kljuic. Stop. Nothing more. It didn't go on. So I take it with the exception of Kljuic, you haven't interviewed anyone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. That's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when the late President Izetbegovic was alive, did you ever interview him at least being an historian to try to find out what was going through his mind during this period, especially when we see sometimes he would say one thing in the morning or agree to something in the morning and maybe change his mind in the afternoon? Did you ever try to meet with the late President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, he was pretty open as well. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Relatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you've made several trips to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, the late President Izetbegovic lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. As does Silajdzic, who probably -- you know, he's an actor that we'll hear about. He's around, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ganic? He's around?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you never availed yourself to any of the key primary sources in order at least to -- to factor in their opinions and their views and their thoughts and their memories along with all the other data in order for you to come up with a historical conclusion for which you want this Trial Chamber to rest upon?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: For better or worse, most every word ever spoken by Mr. Izetbegovic and President Tudjman have been published in interviews and in a host of books which are their collected works, and one of the problems, I think, is asking historical actors about things that happened a long time ago becomes a very difficult proposition because of faded memories. People tend to recall what they have published about what they said rather than what they actually did or said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, for instance, if you were to have someone like Kljuic comes in -- come in and testify, or Mr. Manolic come in and testify, or Mr. Mesic to come and testify, since these are political actors and these are long events that have since passed, we could not necessarily rely on their independent memories? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We should be suspicious maybe?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: One has to make a decision one witness at a time, and in some cases the recollections are crystal clear. In other cases, they are somewhat more hazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you don't know until you meet them, right, and talk to them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't think you know until you listen to them and pose some questions to see what their recollection of events is, and you can then weigh that against external documentation about the time in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And then you would know whether -- to some degree you could see whether they're being honest and truthful with you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It may be less a matter of being honest and truthful than having a crisp recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- Of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Which is why maybe we shouldn't pay too much stock on some of these politicians who will come here in court today or tomorrow and testify on behalf of the Prosecution. We shouldn't necessarily jump to embrace everything that they say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is an argument, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will withdraw the question, Your Honour. I think I've made the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There was no point that was made at all, except Mr. Karnavas's talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, by the way you were asked earlier by Mr. Scott some of the founding fathers of the HDZ. I believe I gave you a couple of names, jogged your memory a little bit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Manolic and Mesic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But let's say with those two since they're still alive, do you know how long they were with the HDZ? I mean, I'm skipping ahead, you know, so we --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I can't recall -- I mean, Mesic is no longer with the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: But I can't recall when he left the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was it before or after the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't recall, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall the date of the Washington Agreement, the year, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was negotiated in February and essentially has an effective date of March of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you don't recall whether he was with the party at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about 1993 or 1992? Was he with the party then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: He certainly was with the party in 1992, was at the session in I believe it was Siroki Brijeg that we spoke of earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And after that, when he left, I just don't recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And was Manolic in during that period as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't recall whether he left --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- whether he was in the party at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we leave the one topic on this historical sources, because I think we have a little bit of time to finish this chapter, as it were, and -- you indicated that a lot of historians disagree on what happened, and generally they disagree on certain events.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They tend to disagree more about the significance or the context of an event than they do about events themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Nevertheless, there are some historians who will deny that event X took place, and others who will assert, yes, event Y took place without, you know, the concurrence of other historians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But for this particular conflict and for the former Yugoslavia and the events that ensued and the break-up and why it broke up and all of that stuff, there is a host of different groups of historians; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm not sure that to call them different groups is correct. I would say there are many historians with many different views on the, for example, issue, the causes of the break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Some of them you can call schools or groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Others, I think, are unique in their understanding or approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Some are maybe pro-Serb?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or pro-Croat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Say may be anti-something, like anti-Serb or anti-Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Some are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Some may -- because I have the list over here. I took the time actually. I was going to walk you through all of this, but for the sake of saving the time, some look at the international -- the role that the internationals played and some are favourable to the internationals and some are disfavourable to them; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And some tend to minimise events while others tend to place a great deal of emphasis on certain events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so within this host of various historical schools, you're just one of them. In some issues you -- you may be right and on some issues you may be -- may be off?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, on some issues I find widespread agreement with my position. On a few issues I find much less agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you say that in looking at your report, if one were to -- if one was well-versed with the literature in this -- in this area, would you say that you have copiously looked at and -- and cited Croatian sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I -- I have cited some Croatian sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Again, I haven't probably copiously looked at much of anything, because that was not my intent starting out the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I noticed that if you go back at the end of your -- when you look at the end notes you seem to rely quite a bit on -- on newspaper articles, particularly Oslobodjenje. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I rely some on the contemporary press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And in most cases I've tried to -- I mean, the ideal situation is to balance a press report with an original document of some sort or another source for a document or memoir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not the case, though, in your report, is it? If we look at some of the footnotes, the end notes, we only see Oslobodjenje as the source; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In some cases you do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, that particular newspaper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little slower, please, again, Mr. Karnavas. Less fast, because the interpreters are having difficulty in following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My apologies again. I'm looking at the clock and I'm looking at all this material. It's not easy but I apologise to the translators again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But Oslobodjenje, I think you left off there. Could you -- could you inform us about this particular newspaper? It was a newspaper; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was a daily newspaper. It was founded in 1943 and functioned as the primary daily newspaper in Bosnia-Herzegovina right up until, I would say, a few years ago when it -- when competitors emerged to challenge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, some might say, some might say that it was -- that during the war or during the period -- I want to say pre-conflict, it became sort of the mouthpiece of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That would be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. They would be wrong.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Oslobodjenje never became the mouthpiece of the SDA or its rival would not have been founded in 1997 by financing sources close to the SDA, namely Dnevni Avaz, and the record of Oslobodjenje throughout the war has been pretty carefully studied in a book called Sarajevo Daily by Tom Gjelten in which he clearly establishes the orientation of that editorial board during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, again I guess it would -- all depends on who you consult. I'm looking at David Rieff, I don't know how you pronounce it, Rieff, Slaughterhouse: Bosnia and the Failure of the West. I'm sure you're familiar with the work?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, he claims that -- and, of course, you cited one, I'm citing another. He claims that Oslobodjenje was sympathetic to the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think in -- in the late spring of 1992 that that's a correct statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Prior to that it is considerably more iffy. I think that Oslobodjenje went through a couple of transformations in its primary editorial formation, never really changed in its commitment to try to be what we've called earlier the newspaper of record, to document important statements and speeches and so on and to cover the Bosnian Assembly. During the war, it certainly became a supporter of -- not a supporter, but it -- it, for example, at times withheld key intelligence data that might have been harmful had the information been released, that is might have been harmful to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, he goes on to say that it -- that it suffered intellectual corruption because its editors supported Alija Izetbegovic and his government uncritically, depicting the Muslims as the good guys and the Serbs as fascist aggressors. Is he wrong when he states that about the -- this particular newspaper?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think, again one has to identify the period in time when that took place. There was, after, let's say, April of 1992 a distinct change in the portrayal of the Serb as Chetniks in -- somewhere around that time, about the time that the conflict broke out. I don't know that it ceased being critical of many of the Muslim players, and indeed, as I said, in Oslobodjenje you can find incredibly even in these wartime periods articles from Tanjug in Belgrade, because that was the best source of information available at the time, and in fact, Tanjug functioned as a primary gatherer of information that was cited in many newspapers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as a general -- I'm not picking on this particular newspaper, but Mark Thompson, in his book Forging War: The Media and Serbia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, are you familiar with that particular author?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He says that the media controlled by the -- by the SDA and the Bosnian government was biased. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Again it depends on exactly what time frame one is speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- but as a general proposition I've read someplace and I can get the citation of an historian that says -- but by and large historians are not the best of historians. It's a source but it's not necessarily. You can't take it at face value, you need to test whatever they're reporting. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, there's three different statements there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Are they historians? No, they're not. Are they an essential source for the historian's work? I would argue this that in period we're talking about, absolutely. Do their statements need to be critically examined before they're used? Absolutely. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just -- since we're on newspapers, I just wanted to touch upon -- I need the Court -- the usher's assistance. I just want to show you one document very quickly. It was mentioned -- it was the Prosecution document P 9539. I just want to bring did to your attention very briefly. We're going to put it on the ELMO. This was already introduced. I just wanted to point out something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we've almost finished our sitting for today, just a few more minutes. It's almost 5.00. Bear that in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because it would be time to get to the bottom of the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What problems?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I'm told it's on the screen. Hopefully it will work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You saw this document earlier today; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you have to forgive me, but I don't -- I can't read this language. If you go down to the -- right there. Thank you -- if you go down, could you -- does it not say that it's the -- somebody recognises Bosnia-Herzegovina under the subtitle? Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The headline is "Four key facts." And the subhead or kicker reads "The founding Assembly was participated in by representatives of Croatia -- the Croatian and Slovenian parties."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Continue.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm losing -- the right-hand side is cut off. [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You're not going to allow the division and re --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The last part of the sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: And it says HDZ recognises Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to end on that note since you brought this in. And the date on this I see from the top it's 27 May, 1990. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With that, thank you, Mr. President. For allowing me for a few moments. I'm just trying to steal a few moments that were taken away from me and I apologise to everyone for keeping them past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And thank you, sir. I'll see you tomorrow morning hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's five past five. We're going to adjourn the meeting and reconvene tomorrow at 9.00, and we're going to work until 1.45 tomorrow. I would like to thank you all. See you again tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
